contributions.text_english: Good afternoon, everybody.

contributions.text_english:
We'll get under way. Before we move ahead with today's agenda, I wish to communicate my ruling in response to the point of order raised by Heledd Fychan MS at the end of the meeting on 23 September 2026. I have had an opportunity to review the Record of Proceedings. My ruling is that the contribution made by Joe Martin MS to the short debate on 23 September breached Standing Order 13.9(v), as it constituted

'disorderly, discriminatory or offensive language or language which detracts from the dignity of the Senedd'.

I want to make it clear that Members of the Senedd are entitled to hold and express strong and differing views. I will defend the rights of all Members to express their perspectives and to challenge that of other Members. It is the nature of parliamentary debate that Members will frequently disagree, and often in a robust manner. However, contributions must comply with the Standing Orders and the required standards of conduct in a parliamentary setting. And they must be grounded in respect for others at all times. This ruling concerns the language used and the manner in which the contribution was expressed, rather than the right to debate the subject matter.

I have written to Joe Martin concerning my ruling, and to require that he ensures that the language used meets the requirements of order and respect in future. That is my ruling.

contributions.text_english: 1. What steps is the Welsh Government taking to ensure that public bodies in Wales comply fully and promptly with their legal obligations on freedom of information and access to personal data? OQ64609
contributions.text_original: 1. Pa gamau y mae Llywodraeth Cymru yn eu cymryd i sicrhau bod cyrff cyhoeddus yng Nghymru yn cydymffurfio'n llawn ac yn brydlon â'u rhwymedigaethau cyfreithiol o ran rhyddid gwybodaeth a mynediad at ddata personol? OQ64609

contributions.text_english: Each public body is responsible for its own compliance with the Freedom of Information Act 2000 and the UK general data protection regulation. The Welsh Government supports good practice through engagement with public bodies, while recognising that compliance is independently overseen and enforced by the Information Commissioner’s Office.
contributions.text_original: Mae pob corff cyhoeddus yn gyfrifol ei hun am gydymffurfio efo Deddf Rhyddid Gwybodaeth 2000 a rheoliad cyffredinol y Deyrnas Unedig ar ddiogelu data. Mae Llywodraeth Cymru yn cefnogi arfer da drwy ymgysylltu efo cyrff cyhoeddus, tra’n cydnabod ac yn adnabod bod cydymffurfio yn cael ei oruchwylio’n annibynnol, ac yn cael ei rymuso gan Swyddfa'r Comisiynydd Gwybodaeth.

contributions.text_english:
Diolch, Brif Weinidog. The right to information is meaningless if citizens have to fight public bodies to simply obtain information that they're legally entitled to. Your own Government recognises the statutory deadlines for freedom of information and subject access requests. 

So, I have a very simple question: does the Welsh Government actually monitor whether devolved public bodies in Wales are complying with those legal obligations, and, if so, will you publish that information? Because, if your Government doesn't even know which public bodies are repeatedly failing to comply with the public's right to information, how can you credibly claim that transparency in Wales is being reinforced, rather than merely advertised?

Diolch, Brif Weinidog. The right to information is meaningless if citizens have to fight public bodies to simply obtain information that they're legally entitled to. Your own Government recognises the statutory deadlines for freedom of information and subject access requests. 

So, I have a very simple question: does the Welsh Government actually monitor whether devolved public bodies in Wales are complying with those legal obligations, and, if so, will you publish that information? Because, if your Government doesn't even know which public bodies are repeatedly failing to comply with the public's right to information, how can you credibly claim that transparency in Wales is being reinforced, rather than merely advertised?

contributions.text_english: As I explained in my initial answer, there is no role for Welsh Government to enforce when it comes to other public bodies in Wales. Every public body itself is responsible for its own compliance with the requirements of the Act, in this respect. It is something that my Government considers to be very important: we take very seriously our own responsibilities under the Act; we perform well according to our responsibilities under the Act. But it is, under that Act, the duty of every public body to make sure that they adhere to the requirements put on them by the Information Commissioner's Office.

contributions.text_english: First Minister, public bodies often like to swerve responding to freedom of information requests, especially if the response might make them look bad. This is something that I have experienced first-hand, and it's something, sadly, that has been raised by many of my constituents in the past. Some organisations often like to keep kicking the can down the road to avoid responding, hoping the person seeking information just simply forgets about it. It's frustrating, especially when public bodies are legally bound to provide information. Clearly, improvements could be made. So, First Minister, I'd like to know what discussions have you had with the Information Commissioner's Office about addressing these concerns. I appreciate the response that you just gave to the worthy Member, but if a public body repeatedly fails to respond on time, what action will this Plaid Cymru Government be taking?

But, ultimately, this is a question around an non-devolved issue that has to be addressed to the ICO itself.

contributions.text_english: 2. Will the First Minister provide an update on the Welsh Government’s plans to review the local government funding formula? OQ64607
contributions.text_original: 2. A wnaiff y Prif Weinidog roi diweddariad ar gynlluniau Llywodraeth Cymru i adolygu fformiwla ariannu llywodraeth leol? OQ64607

contributions.text_english: We have delivered our first 100 days commitment to commission a review of the local government funding formula. Independent research by the Wales Centre for Public Policy, which has been commissioned, complements also an extensive programme of work already under way with local government to review the formula and ensure that it better reflects the real cost of delivering services in different parts of Wales.
contributions.text_original: We have delivered our first 100 days commitment to commission a review of the local government funding formula. Independent research by the Wales Centre for Public Policy, which has been commissioned, complements also an extensive programme of work already under way with local government to review the formula and ensure that it better reflects the real cost of delivering services in different parts of Wales.

contributions.text_english: Diolch, Brif Weinidog. The local government settlement for the current financial year was finalised under the previous Welsh Labour Government, following extensive engagement with local authorities. This used an established formula of complex indicators, including population density, service demand and levels of poverty and deprivation, and work was going on to ensure that that was all updated. The local authorities who received the largest annual increase in funding based on that set formula were Newport, Swansea, Blaenau Gwent, Wrexham and Merthyr Tydfil. Following the recent cost-of-living funding announcement, local authorities are now grappling with the realisation that this Plaid Cymru Government does not believe levels of poverty and service demand should be the greatest determinants of Welsh Government funding to tackle poverty. First Minister, can you confirm which local authorities will not receive extra funding to tackle poverty?

contributions.text_english: I'm grateful for the question, from somebody who held a local government ministerial role and who, in fact, instigated work on looking at the formula. Because there is a sense that, somehow, there needs to be a refining of it, and that refinement needs to take place on a number of different levels. There are issues of deprivation that are predominantly urban in nature, there are issues of deprivation that are predominantly rural in nature, and there are issues of deprivation that are equally relevant to both. What I think is positive in taking this view, which the previous administration also supported, is that we work with local government. There is local government engagement and support for this work that is going on, because, surely, it's a principle that should be important to all of us, that knowing that when Welsh public money, through Welsh Government, is spent, it's spent in a way that is equitable wherever people are.

contributions.text_english: First Minister, councils are being asked to do more every year, but with less. Westminster made them responsible for social care. In Cardiff Bay, new statutory duties keep on coming, and other costs are building up. Swansea Council has already set aside £28 million for equal pay claims. That's £28 million not being spent on schools, not being spent on our roads, and not being spent on social care. Similar claims have already bankrupted Birmingham City Council. These are legally binding costs, yet the formula that shares out local government funding was never designed to account for them. So, First Minister, what consideration is being given to these huge costs in the funding formula, and will you commit that no new duties will be placed on councils without the money to deliver them? Otherwise, it is local services that will be cut.

So, First Minister, what consideration is being given to these huge costs in the funding formula, and will you commit that no new duties will be placed on councils without the money to deliver them? Otherwise, it is local services that will be cut.

contributions.text_english: The Member reflects concerns that no doubt exist right across local government in Wales, and they are concerns that we mirror in Government too. Absolutely, nearly 20 years now of cuts—they used to call it 'austerity', but let's call it what it is—cuts by UK Government, successive Conservative and Labour Governments, have led to the situation where, yes indeed, we are asked to do more with less. What's important to me is that we as a Government work very, very closely with local government, which my Cabinet Minister for local government does day in, day out, recognising the pressures that do exist, taking into consideration always how the decisions and actions and ambitions of this Government do place responsibilities not just on the Welsh Government itself, but on our partners throughout Wales. It is very much a consideration that we bring in to the core of decisions around policy, around spending, because we recognise that, across public life in Wales, be it Welsh Government or local government, these years of cuts are taking their toll. It is by working together cleverly that we can try to work through that on behalf of the people that we represent.

contributions.text_english: Our rural services have been historically underfunded and have failed to accurately reflect the cost of providing rural services. That's why the review of the funding formula this Government is undertaking should be welcomed. But isn't it the reality that this shows the urgent need to change Wales's funding formula from Westminster to ensure fairness and justice, and that everyone in this Chamber should support this Government in that call?
contributions.text_original: Mae ein gwasanaethau gwledig wedi'u tangyllido yn hanesyddol ac wedi methu ag adlewyrchu yn gywir cost darparu gwasanaethau gwledig. Dyna pam y dylid croesawu'r adolygiad o'r fformiwla gyllido y mae'r Llywodraeth yma yn ei wneud. Ond onid y realiti yw bod hyn yn dangos yr angen dybryd i newid fformiwla cyllido Cymru o San Steffan i sicrhau tegwch a chyfiawnder, ac y dylai pawb yn y Siambr yma gefnogi'r Llywodraeth yma yn yr alwad honno?

contributions.text_english: The Member is entirely right. That fundamental weakness in the model makes expenditure decisions, whether for urban or rural areas, disproportionately unfair. It's certainly true that rural communities can face additional costs and challenges in providing public services. The review that's ongoing is considering population sparsity and the rural element of society alongside deprivation and broader pressures on services. What we want to do is to keep a structure in place that reflects real need, and ensure that the whole of Wales can have trust in what we're doing in terms of expenditure decisions within Government.
contributions.text_original: Mae'r Aelod yn hollol iawn. Mae'r gwendid sylfaenol yna yn y model yn gwneud penderfyniadau gwariant, p'un ai ar gyfer ardaloedd trefol neu wledig, yn anghymesur o annheg. Mae'n sicr yn wir y gall cymunedau gwledig wynebu costau a heriau ychwanegol wrth ddarparu gwasanaethau cyhoeddus. Mae'r adolygiad sydd yn digwydd rŵan yn ystyried teneurwydd poblogaeth ac elfen wledig cymdeithas ochr yn ochr ag amddifadedd a phwysau ehangach ar wasanaethau. Beth rydyn ni eisiau ei wneud ydy cadw strwythur mewn lle sydd yn adlewyrchu angen go iawn, a sicrhau bod Cymru gyfan yn gallu cael ymddiriedaeth yn yr hyn rydyn ni'n ei wneud o ran penderfyniadau gwariant mewn Llywodraeth.

contributions.text_english: First Minister, I certainly agree with the comments made by colleagues across the Chamber here so far, because local authorities, councils, and the work they do is the lifeblood of our communities, from the roads that we drive on to the schools that we send our children to. The funding formula is an important aspect of the ability to deliver these services. Another aspect of funding is through council tax rises. In my constituency, Fflint Wrecsam, the local authorities of Flintshire and Wrexham have made significant council tax rises over recent years because of having to fund those services that are vital to people, day in and day out. But I wonder, in considering funding for local authorities, what you think is an acceptable council tax rise for local authorities to make. Will you be considering putting a cap on local authorities in Wales?

But I wonder, in considering funding for local authorities, what you think is an acceptable council tax rise for local authorities to make. Will you be considering putting a cap on local authorities in Wales?

contributions.text_english: It's very important that local authorities are able to make their own decisions on local taxation. I know I have never met a local councillor or a leader of a council who wants to raise council tax in a way that impacts their constituents more than is absolutely necessary. We made a decision around the deal on the budget with the previous Government that absolutely reflected the need to minimise council tax increases, in making sure that we were able to negotiate an agreement that made sure that there was a minimum 4 per cent uplift in order to limit council tax increases. Those decisions are best left for local representatives. That's an important principle.

contributions.text_english: I now call on the party leaders to question the First Minister. First of all, leader of Reform UK, Helen Jenner.

contributions.text_english: Diolch, Lywydd. First Minister, following the serious incident involving an RAF Hawk aircraft on Ynys Môn last week, I'm sure you'll join me in paying tribute to the emergency services who responded so quickly, to the two air crew involved and to everybody at RAF Valley. First Minister, RAF Valley is one of the biggest employers on Ynys Môn, as you know, providing well over 1,000 jobs on the island. The humming of those jets flying overhead is the sound of freedom. In Wales, we are proud to play our part in the defence of the United Kingdom. This brings us greater national security and high-quality, high-skill jobs. I'm grateful to the brave veterans on these benches that I'm lucky to sit alongside as well. And I recognise the sacrifices made because both my brothers are currently serving in the armed forces. This weekend, you spoke at an independence rally in Aberystwyth. You've signed an agreement with separatists, and your programme for government seeks the power to hold a referendum. If you achieve your goal of ripping Wales out of the United Kingdom, what will happen to the people who work at RAF Valley, or any other military sites across Wales, for that matter? First Minister, who will defend our nation?

contributions.text_english: I am grateful to the Member for drawing attention to the response at RAF Valley to the accident last week. I immediately contacted, through my office, the station commander at Valley to wish him and his team at Valley well at what was a very anxious time, and of course to wish a full and rapid recovery to the two airmen who ejected from the aircraft. I believe in defending Wales. Wales has a role to play, of course, within the defence of the United Kingdom. We owe a huge debt of gratitude to those who serve in our armed forces. My attitude will always be to seek ways of working together internationally to strengthen the way that we can step up to the threats that we face, not least from Russia, with the aggression shown towards our European partners, Ukraine.

contributions.text_english: Reform will never be reckless when it comes to defending our nation, and we believe in a strong Wales in a strong United Kingdom. Speaking of large employers in Wales, First Minister, last week we learned that Legal & General, a firm that employs over 2,000 people here in Wales, is set to cut 1,000 jobs across their UK operations and also that Admiral, which has its headquarters here in Cardiff, our only FTSE 100 company, is cutting 500 jobs. Considering you've had more than one meeting with Andy Burnham, I'd be interested to know what representations you've made to him on behalf of large-scale employers here in Wales, because this Siambr assumes that your conversations have included more than just constitutional matters, like getting on with the day job: safeguarding Welsh jobs, lowering NHS waiting lists, improving our education standards and backing our family farms. The people of Wales will rightly question your priorities. When will you stop turning the dial on divisive constitutional politics and instead focus on the task at hand, which is what you've been elected to do by the people of Wales?

contributions.text_english: I shall share with the Member a copy of our programme for government again, which emphasises the way that my Government is dealing every day with the issues that we face on health, on education, on housing, on child poverty, on helping the Welsh family farm. Nobody on our benches is talking Wales down. We believe in a strong Wales in a strong United Kingdom. We have to remember as well that recently, in a poll commissioned by YesCymru, two thirds of people who responded said they did not want an independent Wales. They don't want to be ripped out of the United Kingdom. You have to bear that in mind. It was a YesCymru poll.

You failed to pass your first budget, First Minister, and I'm sure you've learned that, in a minority Government, you have to work with parties around this Chamber to have a hope of passing your financial measures and staying in government. Instead of signing pacts with dangerous separatists, instead of preaching to the converted at independence rallies, you should be making calls to the leaders and finance spokespeople in this Chamber to bring consensus.

The so-called Party of Wales would rather spend the people of Wales’s taxes in Uganda than here at home on our nursing graduates who have been left without jobs and on Welsh pupils with additional learning needs. When will you put aside your personal pet projects and put the people of Wales first?

contributions.text_english:
I think it's useful to be having this conversation in public here to explain, once again, that our intention is to build significantly on what has already been delivered through Flying Start. The Labour leader has often criticised us for being too ambitious in our plans for the roll-out of childcare. We don't apologise for that ambition, but it does mean building on Flying Start, which has helped many families in poverty. There are more families in poverty not being helped by Flying Start than those who are being helped by Flying Start. We say let's help them all. And there's a real danger, I think, in the Labour leader here focusing too much on a name. We want to focus on helping families the length and breadth of Wales, and that is what this Government's plans are all about.

And it's the same with ALN. We have plans in place that we have put on the table, and I again invite the Labour leader to work with us on that, because it's about building on issues that are important to families. My finance Minister has written today to all the party leaders here in the Senedd asking to come together, asking for co-operation. There is still a small window to get out through that door the £40 million on the table that Mark Drakeford suggests you should have taken. It's still an offer, and it's a genuine offer to work co-operatively with you to get that money spent.

First Minister, it's still not enough. We've heard your concerns over many weeks about public finance, which begs the question why you'd squander public money on rebranding Flying Start if the only threat is to its name.

But I'd like to turn to national security. Welsh Government Ministers have to rely on the intelligence of others, and that's because there is no significant intelligence-gathering capability here in Wales. And yet we are obviously, given the news that we've seen this week, being watched very carefully and targeted by Russian and other intelligence agencies, as well as many others who seek to break us. In the interest of national security and in the interest of standing up for the people of Wales, could I ask whether you and indeed the leaders of other groups in this Chamber would agree to receive a comprehensive briefing from intelligence chiefs in the UK defence forces over the specific scale and breadth of threats facing Wales and its people?

contributions.text_english: Diolch, Lywydd. First Minister, I hope you enjoyed your visit to Aberystwyth over the weekend. How do you feel to have recruited Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov to your campaign to break up the United Kingdom? As you know, he's been gleefully speaking about the prospects of referendums on the future of the UK, especially following your meeting with Sinn Féin and the Scottish National Party two weeks ago, which I believe was all over Russian tv. Are you pleased to have Putin's Russia cheerleading on this independence mission that you've set yourself on, or do you finally realise the folly of focusing on that issue and the constitutional navel-gazing, rather than cracking on with improving our sliding educational standards, getting to grips with the crisis in our NHS and trying to fire up the Welsh economy?

First Minister, before the last election to the Senedd, you told the people of Wales that the election was not going to be about independence. Yet since that election, you have done everything to make this Senedd about the issue of independence. You either clearly didn't get the memo that you wrote yourself, or you deliberately misled the people of Wales and tried to get them to vote for Plaid by seeking to dampen down your aspirations for an independent Wales.

Prior to going to those polls in May, back in March, this Senedd—the previous Senedd rather, but the Welsh Parliament—passed legislation. We passed legislation to prevent people lying during election periods. I would remind you that you and your party voted in support of that legislation, and yet still went on to say, 'It's nothing to do with independence, this election', and bark on about it ever since you've arrived back in this place.

When I looked at the scenes on the tv over the weekend, I saw YesCymru claiming that 8,000 people were in attendance at the rally in Aberystwyth—that's a figure, by the way, that I take with a large dose of Halen Môn salt; I'm not really sure it was true. But even if I were to accept that number, do you know the figures that are in my mind? The figures that are in my mind are the 709,000 on an NHS waiting list and the 1 million people in Wales who don't have an NHS dentist. When will you show the same passion and drive to get to grips with those issues as you do for this matter of independence?

I feel as if there's an attempt every week to draw a big rabbit out of a hat that the leader of Plaid Cymru believes in independence for Wales. That doesn't come as a surprise—the fact that the leader of Plaid Cymru, which has campaigned for the right of the people of Wales to decide their own future for 100 years, should give up a couple of hours on a Saturday afternoon to make that case. Because I happen to have a higher level of ambition and belief in my nation than the leader of the Conservatives, who is in cahoots with the leader of Labour and the leader of Reform.

We have in Plaid Cymru a Government that persuaded the people of Wales that we need to step up a gear. But this term in Government isn't about putting forward a referendum on independence. It's not. But is it about making the case for what Wales could be? The people of Wales responded in saying, 'You know what? No, we're not quite with you yet; there's been a massive increase in support for independence, but we're not with you yet.' I get that completely. 'But we like your belief in Wales and we believe that if you believe in Wales that much, you will do everything with the tools that you have now to improve standards on health, to raise education standards, to create jobs in every part of Wales.' That is precisely what this Government has started doing from day one, and I invite him to pay closer attention to that bread-and-butter work that we are doing in this Government.

contributions.text_english: 3. How is the Welsh Government supporting independent and grass-roots music venues to thrive? OQ64587
contributions.text_original: 3. Sut mae Llywodraeth Cymru yn cefnogi lleoliadau cerddoriaeth annibynnol a llawr gwlad i ffynnu? OQ64587

contributions.text_english: Grass-roots music venues are vital to Wales's music sector and to developing the next generation of Welsh talent. Through Creative Wales, we provide direct capital investment to help venues become more sustainable, and work closely with the Music Venue Trust. Eligible grass-roots music venues can now also benefit from the Welsh Government's recently announced support through the non-domestic rates system too.
contributions.text_original: Grass-roots music venues are vital to Wales's music sector and to developing the next generation of Welsh talent. Through Creative Wales, we provide direct capital investment to help venues become more sustainable, and work closely with the Music Venue Trust. Eligible grass-roots music venues can now also benefit from the Welsh Government's recently announced support through the non-domestic rates system too.

contributions.text_english: Diolch, Brif Weinidog. I'd like to declare an interest as co-founder of Saith Seren, an independent music venue. Many grass-roots venues are struggling. We've seen the closure of some much-loved venues across Cymru. We must do more to support this sector. As you mentioned, the 30 per cent business rates cut is a huge step in that direction. It's a great start, but there are more steps that can be taken, I believe, by the UK Government. Last week, I attended an event with Music Venue Trust, which highlighted the issue of value added tax. In my constituency, we've got some great grass-roots music venues, such as The Rockin' Chair in Wrexham and the Tivoli in Buckley. I'm sure you're familiar with both. They provide opportunities for artists to grow and to support creative and economic growth. However, VAT rates are a significant pressure on these venues. In light of this, does the First Minister agree with me that we must urge the UK Government not only to review the VAT threshold faced by this sector, but also to consider a zero-VAT rate on ticket sales?

contributions.text_english:
It's good to hear that the Tivoli is still there. It's about a quarter of a century, I think, since I was there—a great venue. I welcome the Member's support to the campaign, and agree that it's vital that we look at all options to help the viability of our music venues, to encourage economic growth. We recognise the financial pressures, of course, facing venues and the live music sector; that's why we have introduced our new rates relief for this very important sector. I declare an interest as somebody who has played on many a stage myself and realises the value of these venues.

But VAT policy, of course, is a reserved matter. We recognise the concerns raised by the sector around both the VAT registration threshold and the VAT applied to ticket sales and the impact that these absolutely can have on the sustainability of grass-roots venues, but those actions will need to be taken by the UK Government. We will continue, of course, to engage with the sector, including Music Venue Trust, and ensure that the issues facing grass-roots venues in Wales genuinely are understood and represented in our discussions, also, with the UK Government.

contributions.text_english:
I'm glad you brought up this question about music venues, because they are struggling. I want to talk about Arts Council Wales's core funding. Grass-roots music venues seem to get nothing from that, whereas other music genres, like opera, can receive millions of pounds. So, the same system that subsidises theatres and galleries without question tells our small venues that they're commercial operations and they must fend for themselves. We've talked about some of the clubs that are still going, but some have failed—Central Station in Wrexham, TJ's in Newport and Barfly in Cardiff. This month, Tramshed missed out on rates relief by £4,000. Just because business returned to normal after COVID, it doesn't mean they're making more money now.

Every business supports the 30 per cent business rates cut, and we support that here, but these small venues are not taking advantage of that because they're just slightly over the threshold, and we really risk an effect on young Welsh talent. So, I'd like to ask you: can you think about replacing the cliff edge with a taper and commit to parity of esteem for grass-roots music venues? Diolch.

contributions.text_english: 4. Will the First Minister outline how residents in Afan Ogwr Rhondda will benefit from the national energy strategy? OQ64584
contributions.text_original: 4. A wnaiff y Prif Weinidog amlinellu sut y bydd trigolion Afan Ogwr Rhondda yn elwa o'r strategaeth ynni genedlaethol? OQ64584

contributions.text_english: Afan Ogwr Rhondda is an important example, I think, of where, historically, Wales’s natural resources were extracted to power the industrial revolution, with little lasting benefit to the community. Through our national energy strategy and our proposals for a future public energy company, we want to attract investment, support local ownership, create skilled jobs and keep more of the economic value in our communities. That's the lesson of the past.
contributions.text_original: Mae Afan Ogwr Rhondda yn enghraifft bwysig, dwi'n meddwl, o sut cafodd adnoddau naturiol Cymru eu defnyddio yn y gorffennol i bweru'r chwyldro diwydiannol, ond lle doedd yna ddim wedyn ddigon o'r budd economaidd yn aros yn y cymunedau lleol hynny. Drwy ein strategaeth ynni genedlaethol a'n cynigion ar gyfer cwmni ynni cyhoeddus yn y dyfodol, mi ydym ni am ddenu buddsoddiad, cefnogi perchnogaeth leol, creu swyddi da a chadw mwy o'r gwerth yn ein cymunedau. Dyna'r wers o'r gorffennol.

contributions.text_english: Diolch, Brif Weinidog. A key test of this strategy, as you've just outlined, for my constituents is whether the energy transition brings not just more generation, but more good jobs, innovation and economic value to those communities like Afan Ogwr Rhondda. Neath Port Talbot is leading the south-west Wales bid to the UK local innovation partnerships fund, which could be an important addition to those aims. The region was originally told that up to £20 million would be available, but I've now been informed by partners involved that this may have been reduced to £15 million—so by a quarter—while Hull and East Yorkshire and Tees Valley have up to £30 million available jointly. It seems to me the UK Government never seems to miss an opportunity to short-change Wales. Can you confirm whether the Welsh Government has been informed of this change, and what representations will you make to protect south-west Wales's share?

contributions.text_english:
I certainly am aware of the concerns regarding the level of funding available through the local innovation partnerships fund, and officials are already engaging with partners to try to understand the position and any implications for that particular region. We will continue to make the case strongly with the UK Government that Welsh regions should receive a fair share of innovation funding to support high-quality jobs, business growth and energy transition. We believe as a Government in empowering Wales and in empowering the regions of Wales.

The real measure of success isn't simply how much energy we generate with various schemes, but rather how many skilled jobs we create, how many supply chain opportunities are created, and the long-term economic benefits that we create for communities like Afan Ogwr Rhondda. South-west Wales has exceptional strengths in floating offshore wind, industrial decarbonisation, clean energy innovation, and it is vital that investment now reflects and, indeed, releases that potential for future generations.

contributions.text_english: 5. What steps is the Welsh Government taking to increase the use of high-quality washed recycled aggregates in construction projects across Wales? OQ64610
contributions.text_original: 5. Pa gamau mae Llywodraeth Cymru yn eu cymryd i gynyddu'r defnydd o agregau o ansawdd uchel, wedi'u hailgylchu a'u golchi, mewn prosiectau adeiladu ledled Cymru? OQ64610

contributions.text_english: We want more construction material kept in use rather than valuable resources being lost. Wales prioritises recycled and secondary aggregates through planning policy, pushing up the amount of local authority rubble and aggregates that is recycled, and working with the industry too. We are also reviewing how planning and public procurement can create consistent demand for quality-assured recycled materials while protecting safety, performance and of course value for money.

contributions.text_english:
Thank you, First Minister. Wales does need a secure long-term supply of aggregates if we are to deliver the homes, schools, and transport infrastructure our communities need. The Welsh Government has long said that the use of secondary and recycled materials should be maximised where practicable, and high-quality washed recycled aggregates allow us to do exactly that, turning construction and demolition waste into material that meets the same standards as quarried stone and sand, reducing pressure on primary extraction and on marine dredged sand, and cutting carbon all along the way, which is good.

There appears, however, to be a disconnect between Wales's circular economy ambitions and public sector procurement in practice at the moment. We have seen local authority works taking place directly outside a recycling plant in Cwmgwili, where virgin aggregate was sourced from a quarry 20 miles away, rather than using the actual aggregate that was at that plant, which seems ridiculous. We now need action, not words. So, First Minister, what further steps will Welsh Government take through procurement, planning and its own capital programmes to increase the use of washed recycled aggregates in construction projects in Wales?

contributions.text_english: It's an excellent question, Carmelo. First Minister, the latest dedicated national data on construction and demolition waste is from 2019. It estimates that the sector generated 3.43 million tonnes of waste, of which 45 per cent was mixed waste, 38 per cent was soil, and 213,000 tonnes were sent to landfill. There is a measurement, and 'Minerals Technical Advice Note (Wales) 1: Aggregates' remains the detailed national minerals guidance. It specifies that

'Primary aggregates development should not be permitted where...the need could be met at lower environmental cost by the use of secondary or recycled material.'

So, the policy says that we should be moving in this direction. That was put in place in 2004 with a broad objective to increase secondary and recycled sources to at least 25 per cent of supply within five years. We're still hovering around the 25 per cent to 30 per cent mark; I think it's around 28 per cent now. We think that should be higher, and using those—. Again, the Member recognises that we do have tools at our disposal, that we are using them around planning. We need to see how we can make those more effective, because those targets of 22 years ago have been met, but actually we need to find ways of going further.

contributions.text_english: 6. Will the First Minister provide an update on the Welsh Government's discussions with the UK Government regarding further devolution to Wales? OQ64589
contributions.text_original: 6. A wnaiff y Prif Weinidog roi diweddariad ar drafodaethau Llywodraeth Cymru gyda Llywodraeth y DU ynglŷn â datganoli pellach i Gymru? OQ64589

contributions.text_english: The Member knows my view that the current devolution settlement is unfair and unsustainable. During my initial discussions with the Prime Minister in July, I pressed the case for further devolution as a means of improving outcomes for the people of Wales. I'll be doing so again at the National Economic Council next month. I also emphasise that any further devolution must respect the Senedd, not bypass it. And the Cabinet Minister for Finance is also engaging with the UK Treasury in seeking a review of the fiscal framework, Barnett reform and a fair deal from the UK Government's budget, which is in all our interests.

contributions.text_english:
Diolch. Although conversations with UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham have so far been positive in terms of devolution, it's clear that we need to reiterate to Westminster that we are a country and not a county. Devolution to the devolved nations is clearly not the same as devolution to the English regions. As Chair of the Constitution, Justice and External Affairs Committee, I wrote last week to Andy Burnham to invite him to give evidence to our committee to explain his priorities for devolution in Cymru.

The Welsh Government has been clear that we need parity of powers with Scotland as a basic, in order to do the day job—something that others in this Chamber seem to struggle to understand. We need more borrowing powers in order to invest in services and infrastructure here; the devolution of policing and justice in order to align policy in order to deliver better outcomes; and basic fairness with powers over rail and the Crown Estate. We will no longer tolerate a third-rate devolution settlement. So, can the First Minister outline what discussions he's having with the UK Government to make that clear?

contributions.text_english:
I agree very much, obviously, that devolution to Wales as a nation is not the same as devolution within England, and our starting point is that Wales should have the powers and resources needed to deliver for the people of Wales, and absolutely that includes parity with Scotland as a minimum, where doing so would improve outcomes for citizens and strengthen democratic accountability.

Plaid Cymru is a party that has always supported and promoted the notion of empowering the communities of Wales. That's our call now, but we have to have an empowered Senedd, an empowered Welsh Government, in order to deliver what is right for communities the length and breadth of Wales. We've made that case consistently to UK Government, pressing for progress in areas including justice and policing, rail infrastructure, the Crown Estate and fiscal powers, and we will continue to engage constructively with UK Government, because this is about acting in the best interests of the people of Wales. It is about health, it is about education, it is about job creation and it is about fighting poverty.

We are here, being able to fight for the people of Wales, because a decision was made to devolve. We are here, able to create laws for the people of Wales, because a decision was then made to enhance that devolution. I still think it's an ongoing process, looking for ways that we can better support the people that we are here to represent.

contributions.text_english: Tackling child poverty and securing the best future for every child in Wales is at the heart of our programme for government. We are creating a new strategy to tackle child poverty. We're setting clear targets and milestones to drive ambitious, deliverable change. We're also introducing a new ambitious childcare offer to support families with the cost of living and are developing the Cynnal child payment pilot as part of a suite of measures.

contributions.text_english:
Diolch, Brif Weinidog. In Blaenau Gwent, 48.6 per cent of children live in income deprivation. That's the highest rate of any local authority in Wales, and it's just so heartbreaking and unacceptable that in twenty-first century Wales so many of our children are growing up without the opportunities that every child deserves. We know that growing up in poverty can have a lasting impact on a child's health, their education and opportunities, shaping their life chances well into adulthood. 

That's why I really do welcome the ambition of this Plaid Cymru Government to make child poverty a defining mission. It's a moral imperative, because every child deserves the same opportunities in life regardless of where they're born. So, as this Government takes a much needed and ambitious new approach, how will you make sure that this ambition translates into real change for children and families in Blaenau Gwent Caerffili Rhymni?

Last week, I, alongside a number of Senedd Members, met veterans who were on the Sir Galahad and their families, and families of soldiers who lost their lives on that most awful day in Welsh history. Thank you for your answer, First Minister. I would like to follow that keenly. As a veteran myself, we need to know when we deploy that our people and our Government have our backs.

Over the past few months, many veterans have been stating to me that the messaging coming out from the Governments at both ends of the M4 is very confusing. Both seem to state that they care, but when put under the microscope, a different tale begins to emerge. Over recent weeks in this Chamber, we've seen you calling Sinn Féin your sister party—the political arm of the IRA who were responsible for 24 soldiers' deaths linked to Welsh regiments, including the Welsh Guards, and numerous casualties in Northern Ireland. Next, we see the ethical framework that might risk vital equipment getting into the hands of those fighting on our behalf.

Numerous cases are being reported to MSs across this Chamber, and I have a couple, on the ongoing assistance for veterans who, despite councils signing up to the armed forces covenant, are being left wanting: a veteran who has had to sleep with their own mother, in the same bed, for eight years, for lack of getting a house; a recovering alcoholic placed above a pub; homeless veterans having to prove that they've rough-slept for three to four days before assistance will even begin. Does the First Minister agree with me that this is simply not good enough, and a betrayal of those who have fought for our safety?

contributions.text_english: 10. What are the Welsh Government’s constitutional priorities for Wales? OQ64572
contributions.text_original: 10. Beth yw blaenoriaethau cyfansoddiadol Llywodraeth Cymru ar gyfer Cymru? OQ64572

contributions.text_english: The current devolution settlement is outdated, constrains our economic potential and hinders our ability to deliver the best public services to people in Wales. Our immediate constitutional priorities are the devolution of policing and justice, the Crown Estate and rail infrastructure, alongside fair funding and greater fiscal flexibility. As a matter of principle, there is certainly no reason why powers that have been devolved to Scotland shouldn't also be devolved to Wales.

contributions.text_english: Diolch. The latest YouGov polling, conducted between 7 and 13 September this year, found that just 20 per cent of people in Wales support Welsh independence—the lowest recorded level since 2023. Meanwhile, 72 per cent of people in Wales reported dissatisfaction with the NHS, 57 per cent of Welsh voters placed the economy among their three most important issues, and, furthermore, 20 per cent of pupils leave primary school functionally illiterate, whilst Wales remains at bottom of the UK Programme for International Student Assessment rankings. First Minister, it has been pointed out by our colleague here, Helen Jenner. It has been pointed out by many other Members. We represent those very people who put us here in this Senedd. With no parliamentary majority for it here in the Senedd—and I’d defy you to prove me otherwise—why is constitutional change taking priority for you, above fixing our NHS, fixing our economy and fixing our schools? It's a downright disgrace.

I congratulate the Member for being drawn out of the lot to ask a question to the First Minister again. I don't know why she chooses not to ask a question about health, to not ask a question about education, to not ask a question about strengthening the Welsh economy, supporting the family farm, bringing children out of poverty. I think those are the really important issues that are important to the people of Wales, and I believe that empowering Wales to have more tools at our disposal to deal with education, health, job creation and farming is a good thing. The Member is here because we have devolution. She is able to make the case for her constituents because we have devolution. And, as I said earlier, she is able to put forward legislation because we have enhanced devolution. 

There is a reality here that we are seeing an obsession with wanting to stop Wales being empowered. The Member has to reflect upon what that says about her. Because I will always want Wales to have the best possible crack at the whip, and that means making sure that we have the tools to do the job for the people of Wales. I'll use the word again: there's an obsession with making damn sure that Wales doesn't get any more ability to get to grips with those issues that really matter to the people of Wales.

contributions.text_english: Our ambition is for everyone in Wales to have access to good-quality affordable housing in the right area for them. contributions.text_english: Thank you, First Minister. The Home Office has written to me confirming that around 70 homes are currently being used for asylum seekers in north-east Wales. That's up 25 per cent on 2025-26. Now, 283 people are housed in this area—that's 43 more than the same time last year. And now the Home Office is looking to move more in. Opposition in villages and towns across north-east Wales is strong, and there is no surprise in that when you consider that 650 local people are still being housed in hotels and bed and breakfasts. I was shocked when a county council in Clwyd explained to me that, often, asylum seekers are moved in without prior notification to the local authority—they're finding out after the fact. First Minister, do you agree with me that local authorities should be consulted before asylum seekers are moved in, and that locals should always be prioritised for housing?

contributions.text_english: I don't hesitate in saying that of course I recognise where there are genuine concerns in communities. My colleagues and I have spoken widely about the need for the Home Office to have dispersal processes in place that reflect the needs and pressures of communities, and the needs of people who are within the asylum system. But those are matters for the Home Office. I will deal with these issues always in a way that tries to calm the discussion, tries to deal with facts, recognising genuine concerns. But, ultimately, our powers aren't around how many people come to Wales. Ours are about recognising what our values are as a nation. When people do come here, we want to make sure that they are able—for everybody in society in Wales—to integrate properly.

Trefnydd, I'd like to request a statement from the Welsh Government regarding the impact of rising energy and fuel costs on Welsh households and businesses. According to RAC Fuel Watch, the average price of diesel has now reached around £2 per litre, and the average price of petrol is around £1.74 per litre. In rural constituencies like Ceredigion Penfro, the increase in fuel prices has a particularly big knock-on effect, as many people have little choice but to rely on their vehicles to access work, healthcare and essential services. These increases are placing significant pressure on families and businesses at a time when many are already struggling with the rising cost of living, and it also has serious consequences for businesses, hauliers and farmers, by squeezing what are already very tight margins.

I appreciate that the Welsh Government is not responsible for fuel duty, but it does have some responsibility around energy policy. So, Trefnydd, given the impact of rising fuel and energy costs on Welsh households and businesses, I'd be grateful if we could have a statement from the Welsh Government outlining what representations have so far been made to the UK Government ahead of the autumn budget regarding fuel duty and energy costs, and what support is available in Wales to help those who are struggling as a result of these increases.

contributions.text_english: Last week, I met with residents in Gwaelod-y-garth impacted by flooding caused by nearby quarry blasting, as well as the quarry operator and other elected representatives. Residents are living in fear that there's this huge body of water sitting above their village, and the quarry is about to restart blasting imminently, before the Health and Safety Executive investigation is even complete. Residents are traumatised by the events that happened this summer and are scared to hear another blast happening above their village. So, can I please ask the Cabinet Minister for Rural Resilience and Sustainability to make representations to the UK Government and Cardiff Council about steps they can take to ensure the safety of quarries and quarry blasting in and around Cardiff, particularly given investigations aren't complete? And please could the Government provide a statement on what it's doing to ensure the safety of those living near quarries, to prevent this from ever happening again? Diolch.

contributions.text_english: I'd like to call for a statement from the Welsh Government on the Global Centre of Rail Excellence, please. Around £70 million of public money has reportedly already gone into the GCRE, including £50 million from the Welsh Government, yet the main rail facility has still not been built. Private investment has not materialised as anticipated, and the future of the project is now under review. I understand the Public Accounts and Public Administration Committee is now asking the Permanent Secretary how that investment has been used and what further funding may be required, and about the Welsh Government's commitment to support the company's liabilities until September 2027. As shadow Minister for Government efficiency, I believe taxpayers deserve answers too. Will the Government therefore make a statement setting out exactly what public money has been spent and what it has delivered; what financial controls, reviews and value for money assessments were undertaken; what timescales and funding assumptions changed; and what further exposure taxpayers may face? Before another penny is committed, the Senedd deserves a clear account of the money already spent and the decisions behind it.

contributions.text_english: Trefnydd, I would like to request a statement on the shameful neglect of some of Wales's most treasured historic sites, including our Roman remains in Caerwent, known to the Romans as Venta Silurum. That makes their condition even more disgraceful, that what should be a source of national pride is now being swallowed by weeds—nearly 2,000 years of history left to deteriorate under successive Governments' watches here. As you know, Trefnydd, these sites are vital to our history, education and tourism in Monmouthshire and across Wales. Bizarrely, I asked for an urgent meeting with Cadw about their condition, and was told to ask you first for permission for a meeting. I'm not sure if that's normal. Trefnydd, can I request a statement from you on the upkeep of historic sites in Wales? And can I cheekily use this opportunity to invite you there yourself to see the disgraceful condition that they're in? Diolch.

contributions.text_english:
Can I call for two statements today, please, Trefnydd? The first is from the Cabinet Minister for Health and Care in relation to Martha's law. As you will know, following the tragic death of Martha Mills, a 13-year-old in England who died of sepsis in 2021, the English NHS is benefiting from the roll-out of Martha's law in emergency departments, in maternity settings, in all in-patient settings. We have a similar approach in Wales, but people are less familiar with it, because it isn't called Martha's law or Martha's rule. And I wonder to what extent the Welsh Government could look at just adopting it lock, stock and barrel to make sure that patients here have the benefit of being able to call for that immediate clinical review of their patients, if they're concerned about patient safety.

Secondly, can I call on the Cabinet Minister for Enterprise, Connectivity and Energy on the rising costs of fuel, particularly in relation to home-to-school transport operators, many of whom now are really struggling to make ends meet with the viability of some of the routes that they are supporting, getting kids to and from school? Conwy, Denbighshire and Flintshire councils have all been approached for support by home-to-school operators in the constituency that I represent, but, unfortunately, they do need that national direction from either the Welsh Government or the UK Government in order that they can get the resources that they need to make sure that these routes are still viable.

I know that the Cabinet Minister for Health and Care would be more than happy to discuss this further with you directly. I'm sure that we are united in terms of those calls. contributions.text_english: I'd like to request a statement on the well-being outcomes for care leavers in Wales. Last month, the UK Department of Education published 'You really are on your own', a study of the early deaths of young people who were in care, and its findings are deeply concerning. In 2025 alone, 112 care leavers aged 18 to 24 died in England, an estimated death rate around three to four times that of their peers in the general population. One in five of those deaths occurred at age 18, right when support so often fails and falls away. The report must serve as a warning for us here in Wales. Care-experienced young people have consistently raised here many of the issues around isolation, cliff edges in support, and independence being treated as more important than well-being. So, may I ask, please, Trefnydd, what can we do here in Wales to make sure we've got the data on young people and make sure we've got the services in place to support them? Diolch yn fawr iawn.

contributions.text_english: Business Minister, can I please request a statement from the Cabinet Minister for Health and Care about the potential withdrawal of funding for specialist cerebral palsy therapy services within the Aneurin Bevan health board? Families across my constituency are facing deep uncertainty and concern as the health board reviews its service level agreement with Cerebral Palsy Cymru. While other health boards across Wales, including Cwm Taf Morgannwg, Swansea Bay and Hywel Dda, continue to secure access to this highly specialist intervention, children in my constituency risk being left behind. Local NHS therapy teams perform vital work, but they lack the specific advanced training, experience and clinical capacity required to replicate the specialised care provided by Cerebral Palsy Cymru. Withdrawing this contract creates an unacceptable postcode lottery, and also threatens the early intervention programmes that have provided crucial early years support to 79 babies in the Aneurin Bevan area at zero cost to the NHS or Welsh Government, a move that directly contradicts this Government's own preventative health agenda. Decisions like this actively undermine early intervention, harm long-term development outcomes, and place an unfair burden on families. So, will the Cabinet Secretary make an urgent statement outlining how the Welsh Government will intervene to protect these vital services, eliminate a postcode lottery, and commit to a sustainable national pathway for children with cerebral palsy? Thank you.

Local NHS therapy teams perform vital work, but they lack the specific advanced training, experience and clinical capacity required to replicate the specialised care provided by Cerebral Palsy Cymru. Withdrawing this contract creates an unacceptable postcode lottery, and also threatens the early intervention programmes that have provided crucial early years support to 79 babies in the Aneurin Bevan area at zero cost to the NHS or Welsh Government, a move that directly contradicts this Government's own preventative health agenda. Decisions like this actively undermine early intervention, harm long-term development outcomes, and place an unfair burden on families. So, will the Cabinet Secretary make an urgent statement outlining how the Welsh Government will intervene to protect these vital services, eliminate a postcode lottery, and commit to a sustainable national pathway for children with cerebral palsy? Thank you.

contributions.text_english: Thank you for raising that issue. But these are individual decisions for health boards, and that is why I would urge you to raise these issues, so that it's part of our consideration in looking at the preventative services available and how we secure equal access, wherever you live in Wales, to those services.

contributions.text_english:
Thank you very much, Llywydd. I'm pleased to provide an update on the commitment in our first 100-day plan to commission a review of the effectiveness of the NHS Wales escalation and intervention framework.

The review was commissioned to ensure that our arrangements for accountability, oversight, support and intervention remain fit for purpose in a healthcare environment that is increasingly complex. Discussions with NHS organisations in recent months have reinforced the need for a framework that is clearer, more consistent, and more focused on securing sustainable improvement.

The review found that escalation and intervention arrangements provided an important mechanism for identifying concerns, strengthening oversight, and deploying targeted support where necessary. However, the review also found opportunities to strengthen the connection between routine accountability processes and formal intervention arrangements. In particular, there was a desire to move away from a system that is perceived primarily through the lens of escalation levels to a new system, a system that places greater emphasis on continuous assessment and early intervention, helping organisations to improve and, ultimately, ensures better outcomes for patients.

Today, we publish a new accountability and support framework, which provides a single, coherent approach to deal with accountability, assurance, support and intervention across NHS Wales. It establishes a more transparent and structured framework that will help the Welsh Government and NHS organisations to assess how they are performing, identify emerging risks, and agree the responses required to support improvement. It also clarifies better the relationship between accountability meetings, routine performance oversight, improvement support and intervention activity.

Mi gafodd yr adolygiad ei gomisiynu i sicrhau bod ein trefniadau ar gyfer atebolrwydd, goruchwyliaeth, cymorth ac ymyrraeth yn dal yn addas i'r diben mewn amgylchedd gofal iechyd sy'n mynd yn fwyfwy cymhleth. Mae trafodaethau efo sefydliadau'r GIG dros y misoedd diwethaf wedi atgyfnerthu'r angen am fframwaith sy'n gliriach, yn fwy cyson, ac yn canolbwyntio'n fwy ar sicrhau gwelliant cynaliadwy.

Mi ddaeth yr adolygiad i'r casgliad bod trefniadau uwchgyfeirio ac ymyrraeth yn chwarae rhan bwysig wrth nodi pryderon, cryfhau goruchwyliaeth, a darparu cymorth wedi'i dargedu lle bo angen. Er hynny, mi wnaeth yr adolygiad hefyd nodi cyfleoedd i gryfhau'r cysylltiad rhwng prosesau atebolrwydd arferol a threfniadau ymyrryd ffurfiol. Yn benodol, roedd awydd i symud oddi wrth system sy'n canolbwyntio'n bennaf ar lefelau uwchgyfeirio at system newydd, system sy'n rhoi mwy o bwyslais ar asesu parhaus ac ymyrryd yn gynnar, helpu sefydliadau i wella ac, yn y pen draw, sicrhau canlyniadau gwell i gleifion.

Heddiw, rydym ni'n cyhoeddi fframwaith atebolrwydd a chymorth newydd, sy'n cyflwyno un dull clir a chydlynol o ymdrin ag atebolrwydd, sicrwydd, cymorth ac ymyrraeth ledled gwasanaeth iechyd cenedlaethol Cymru. Mae'n sefydlu fframwaith cliriach a mwy tryloyw sy'n helpu Llywodraeth Cymru a sefydliadau'r GIG i asesu sut maen nhw'n perfformio, nodi risgiau'n gynnar, a chytuno ar y camau sydd eu hangen i gefnogi gwelliant. Mae hefyd yn egluro'n well sut mae cyfarfodydd atebolrwydd, trefniadau goruchwylio perfformiad arferol, cymorth i wella a gweithgarwch ymyrryd yn cyd-fynd efo'i gilydd.

contributions.text_english:
At its heart, the framework establishes a stronger focus on organisational maturity, capability and sustainable improvement. The framework is structured around the core pillars and domain of leadership and organisational effectiveness, quality, delivery and performance, workforce, and finance and planning. This reflects the reality that organisational challenges rarely exist in isolation and often require a system-wide understanding of the factors influencing performance and outcomes.

The framework also supports a more proactive approach to intervention. Rather than waiting for issues to become deeply embedded, it provides enhanced mechanisms for earlier identification of risk and earlier deployment of support. The intention is that organisations are helped to address challenges before they become more significant and before formal escalation becomes necessary. This is particularly important given the pressures facing NHS Wales, including increasing demand, workforce challenges, financial constraints and the need to continue improving quality and patient outcomes.

This preventative approach is consistent with the wider direction of Government and health policy, which places strong emphasis on earlier action, reducing avoidable harm and supporting long-term sustainability. In practical terms, this means moving from late action when performance has already deteriorated to earlier identification of risk and targeted support before concerns become entrenched. The framework works within the current legislative framework and takes us as far as we can within it, using the powers and levers available to strengthen accountability, deploy support earlier and secure improvement for patients and communities.

A key principle underpinning the framework is that intervention and support should always be purposeful, proportionate and time bound. Enhanced monitoring, oversight and support arrangements should not exist for their own sake. Instead, they should support organisations to deliver measurable improvements, strengthen leadership capability, improve governance arrangements and address the underlying causes of poor performance.

Equally, organisations receiving support should be able to demonstrate progress within an agreed time frame, with decisions about escalation, continuation of support or de-escalation informed by clear evidence and objective assessment. Recent discussions regarding de-escalation arrangements have reinforced the importance of ensuring that improvement is sustained and that appropriate surveillance arrangements remain in place following any reduction in oversight.

Another important development within the framework is the strengthening of accountability arrangements. The revised approach seeks to make expectations clearer for NHS organisations while providing greater consistency in how evidence is reviewed and how organisational assurance is assessed. It also promotes a more comprehensive view of organisational performance, drawing together information from across the various domains to support a rounded assessment of organisational health and capability.

The review has also highlighted the importance of leadership, culture and governance in determining organisational success. Recent discussions concerning organisational performance have repeatedly demonstrated that sustainable improvement is dependent not only on operational delivery, but also on strong leadership, effective governance and a culture that supports openness, learning and accountability.

contributions.text_english:
Importantly, the framework recognises that accountability and support are two sides of the same coin. Organisations must continue to be held accountable for delivering high-quality, safe and sustainable services, but they must also have access to the right support when challenges emerge. That's why the framework seeks to balance constructive challenge with practical support, using expertise to help organisations improve. The aim is to help organisations build their own capability to improve, rather than creating dependency on external oversight.

The framework was developed through engagement between Welsh Government officials, NHS organisations and key stakeholders. It reflects a shared ambition to strengthen accountability, improve transparency and support organisations to achieve sustained improvement for the populations they serve.

The review of the old framework and the development of the new framework represents an important step forward in the way that we oversee performance and help organisations improve across NHS Wales. The new framework brings together accountability, escalation and improvement support into a single integrated system. It provides clearer accountability, more proportionate oversight and earlier support where risks emerge. That helps to strengthen transparency and focus on ensuring better outcomes for patients, staff and communities across Wales. 

Ultimately, the aim of these changes is to give the people of Wales greater confidence that NHS services will receive the necessary support to respond to challenges and improve. The new framework will help identify issues earlier, provide more consistent support to organisations, and ensure that concerns are addressed in a timely and transparent way. For patients and communities, this means services that are better, safer and more reliable, more consistent care, and ensuring that everyone receives the treatment and support that they deserve. Thanks.

contributions.text_english: Thank you, Cabinet Minister, for giving us advance sight of the statement.

contributions.text_english:
I'm glad that we are talking about the escalation framework today, because it's clear to me that the current framework is, frankly, ineffective. Health boards across Wales are sitting in level 4 for certain parts of their domains, or indeed, in the case of Betsi Cadwaladr, level 5, and meanwhile waiting lists continue to go up across the country and patients are not seeing the improvements that they deserve.

There are things in the statement today and within the review, however, that I do agree with. I fundamentally agree with the outcomes for patients being put at the centre of this review, and alongside the outcomes for patients, the addition of the workforce as one of the key pillars within this framework, as I think one thing that is mentioned less than it should be is that the performance of the NHS is not just letting down the patients who depend on it, but it's also letting down those front-line staff who often have to bear the brunt of the frustrations of people interacting with the system.

I also agree that proactivity in intervention should be the objective. We should be ensuring that these health boards are held to a higher quality of standard before the issues arise, and not be seeking to administer remedial action after the issues have already arisen.

One thing that is also mentioned in your statement that I do agree with is the importance of leadership and governance in determining the success of organisational capacity, alongside strengthening accountability for leadership within our health organisations. We at Reform were clear that those who operate our health boards should be held accountable for the performance within them, and we would have considered, if necessary, amending the National Health Service (Wales) Act 2006 to ensure that ministerial authority can be held over these health boards, and if necessary, link pay to performance when it comes to some of these health board bosses who are earning large salaries but failing to deliver for our people.

It's obviously up to Ministers to make the important decisions, and that's something that's outlined in this new framework, but when I was reading through it earlier, there were a couple of occasions where it seemed to me that lines were blurred between Welsh Government taking meetings and providing information versus Ministers. So, I'd like to ask for clarity in terms of where the line drawn is with this new framework. Where will civil servants or other members working for the Government be taking meetings with health boards, and when will meetings be taken by you or your Deputy Ministers?

I'd also like to ask how the lessons learned from intervening with these health boards are being learned and how they will be applied across other health boards in Wales, so that we don't have to keep coming back and deal with the same interventions time and time again.

Another thing that's mentioned in the new framework today is escalation boards. So, once these health boards are put into level 3 or above, escalation board meetings can be held. But there was detail lacking, from what I could read, in terms of how frequent these escalation board meetings will be, what will be discussed within them, and who will be doing the discussing and the decision making within those meetings.

Criteria were also given in terms of de-escalation within the framework, but in terms of the criteria that I read, these were illustrative criteria. So, I'd like to ask: how will the final criteria be determined? I assume they'll be on a case-by-case basis. And who will be determining the criteria both for escalation and de-escalation through the new framework?

Finally, it's mentioned that, in level 5, there will be consideration given to changes of governance within health boards and, at level 4, that there will be leadership and organisational assessments that will be conducted with regard to the leadership of these health boards. So, I would like to ask: how will these assessments be conducted? Who will be reviewed, and on what criteria will they be reviewed by? If, as is the case for many of our health boards across the country, a health board has been sat in level 4 or, indeed, level 5 for an extended period of time, at what point will the Government intervene and pursue organisational changes within the health boards, to ensure that those who are failing to deliver for our patients in Wales are held to account? Diolch yn fawr.

I welcome you to your post and congratulate you on your appointment as shadow spokesperson for health and care. Good luck with it. I thank your predecessor as well for his contributions. 

I welcome the fact that you see the value of what we've put forward here, and that you welcome much of what we've put forward. I would hope that we would have cross-party support for what we are hoping to achieve here. You mentioned putting outcomes at the centre of what we want to achieve, that workforce is important and that we take proactive action, which is all about making sure that we deal with issues before they become major problems that impact on the health outcomes of our people. But you did raise some questions and I'll try my best to respond to as many of them as I can in the few minutes I have.

On the blurred lines you mentioned between civil servants and the Minister, ultimately, my civil servants and officials have meetings regularly with health boards, on a weekly basis, and the director general of the NHS will have regular meetings with the chief executives of health boards.

When it comes to an escalated level and when we need to look at specific issues within health boards, the agreement on how we escalate them and which matters need to be looked at will be come to between Audit Wales, Healthcare Inspectorate Wales, the Welsh Government and the health boards themselves, so that they are an equal partner in this, that they realise what the issues are, and that they come up with solutions with other partners and stakeholders. Then, the work will be led by NHS Wales Performance and Improvement.

NHS Wales Performance and Improvement will lead that work, but, going on to another question you asked about ensuring that lessons are learnt, they will then take those lessons and, in another health board or trust, if an issue arises, they will take those lessons and use them in the learnings for the problems that might arise in other health boards.

The assessments that you mentioned and what criteria will be set will be judged by those stakeholders, including the health boards, but they will be transparent so that people can have confidence in the process. We know in the previous process, it was accused of being used as a political weapon more often than not. This shouldn't be about politics—this should be about making sure that health boards improve if they have problems and de-escalate when they can, so that people can have confidence in the healthcare that they receive. The process will be transparent, assessments will be made by the stakeholders transparently, collectively, and then the de-escalation process will also be transparent and show accountability for the process and how they have come to the judgements they've got for de-escalation purposes.

I think that has responded to most of the questions you asked, at least.

Minister, thanks for the update today on the review of the escalation and intervention framework. One thing that remains unclear to me is around the difference in outcome. What is the difference that you hope to achieve or would expect, and what will the new framework do that couldn't already be done? Furthermore, what exactly are the enhanced mechanisms for earlier identification of risk, and what does earlier deployment of support look like in reality?

Turning to the brilliant workforce within the NHS, what additional staffing and resources will be made available, and will there need to be further expertise and funding to go alongside the new framework? If so, who will provide those resources? Will it come from health board budgets, or will it come via the Welsh Government through Welsh Government budgets? Where health boards fail to improve under this new framework, what happens next and who will be held accountable ultimately?

Patients want to know that when they go into a hospital they're getting the best possible care, and that they're being treated as quickly as possible. How does this framework help with that? What measurable improvements, for example, will there be in safety, access and quality that patients should expect, and how long until they see those?

Finally, waiting lists are still a major problem. They've been going up month after month recently. So when will we see improvements and how will this statement today, and the new framework, help in driving down waiting lists? Diolch.
