contributions.text_english:
Thank you for those questions. They are fair questions. I think when you look at what we are proposing and how we propose to improve outcomes, it states early in the document that the difference between this framework and the previous one is that we have clearer thresholds, there's less duplication, there's greater transparency there, and we have an early identification of risk. So, when a health board or a health trust goes into level 2, we identify early on that there's a problem and ensure that it doesn't become a level 3 or a level 4, and we put that intervention in at an earlier stage. There's a stronger focus on outcomes, rather than just dealing with a crisis when it hits. We make sure that we deal with something earlier on so that those outcomes, whether it be ambulance times or urgent and emergency care or finance and performance, are seen at an earlier stage, and that there are better outcomes in that respect.

More importantly, it also looks at the patient experience and takes on board patient experience. So that is factored into it. It looks at those four key themes, as I said, so there is the quality of service that is crucial in determining if a health board is escalated. The workforce, and the impact on the workforce, is another pillar. The finance and planning delivery and performance is a third pillar, and the leadership, the culture set there, is crucial when it comes to deciding whether or not they can be de-escalated or need to be escalated further. That's what came through in the review, that's what health boards and health managers and people working in the sector themselves told us they thought was missing—ensuring that we have the proper leadership in place.

If I can just make a side note, you mentioned people going to hospitals. I would suggest that we move away from just thinking about hospitals, because the framework looks at all health trusts and health boards, and the health boards delivering primary care as well, primarily. We've got patients that need to look at care closer to home. It also looks at the performance of a health board and the finances of a health board, not just the delivery of services. But absolutely, what we will see is, when a board is put into an escalated measure, there will be transparency around that, so patients know what to expect, what level they're at and what work is being carried out.

You ask about what further resource is put into it. As you will know from your time in Government—I presume that you will have seen some of the Cabinet papers by former health Ministers—hundreds of millions of pounds have been put into supporting health boards over the years, so a level of support will be put in there, there's no change in that respect, but the delivery will be carried out by NHS Wales Performance and Improvement. They are currently carrying out a well-led review with us in Betsi Cadwaladr. NHSPI will then be equipped to make sure that, if work needs to be done, if something needs to be done on let's say cancer outcomes, they can go in with a specialist to help deliver that improvement that's needed in a certain health board or trust.

contributions.text_english:
I thank the Cabinet Minister for his statement this afternoon. Reviewing the escalation and intervention framework is an incredibly important piece of work, and patient outcomes should be at the heart of this. Let's be totally honest: existing arrangements have failed in the past. They have not delivered the sustained improvement that patients and staff rightfully deserve and need.

If we use Betsi Cadwaladr University Health Board as an example, it has been in the highest level of intervention for several years now, and things sadly aren't improving. In fact, it was reported only last week that Betsi reported 13 never events, which are serious, largely preventable incidents that should not be happening at all. Betsi has spent longer in special measures than any other organisation in the history of the NHS. This is a damning indictment of the current framework. So, Cabinet Minister, my question is simple: what are your plans doing to deliver the much-needed improvements?

Sticking with Betsi just for a minute, in June this year, Cabinet Minister, you gave the health board a final chance to improve. You said that all options were on the table as you were sick and tired of the health board being a byword for dysfunction and declining standards. So, will the Cabinet Minister provide an update on the current situation and where you expect Betsi to fall under this new framework?

We also know that special measures and health board interventions can be used as a political tool, as we saw, unfortunately, with the Labour politicians here in the Chamber. Take Vaughan Gething, for example: during his time as health Minister he removed Betsi from special measures just before the 2021 Senedd election in what I can only describe as a desperate attempt to curry favour with voters. So, can I get a commitment from you today, Minister, that this Government will not fall under the same trap as Mr Gething and will not use these interventions for political gain? 

Cabinet Minister, you've set out your ambitions going forward, but this afternoon's statement was a little bit light for me on the detail of what the review unearthed. Perhaps you can elaborate on that for us, please, here in the Chamber. Was the problem the escalation criteria, the speed at which previous Governments acted, the quality of information available, or a broader failure to hold health boards to account when agreed improvements were not delivered? The Cabinet Minister has spoken about the need for earlier intervention when things start going wrong, so what will trigger intervention earlier, and how will the Government act swiftly to prevent situations becoming embedded within health boards?

We all want to see improvements, and I hope for the sake of patients and staff that this is a success, but what happens if the interventions don't work? As I've already said, Betsi has been in some form of special measures for years, so I'm really curious to know what your backup plan is when agreed improvements are not delivered, Minister. At what point does this Government move from supporting a health board to directing it? And will any additional powers become available as part of this new framework?

Finally, Cabinet Minister, how will you monitor the success of your new framework? Anyone who knows me knows that I love a good KPI, so what are your KPIs? In my mind, the only way this will be judged successful is if it leads to genuine improvements for patients, rather than just changing how many health boards are moved between escalation levels. Thank you very much.

contributions.text_english:
Thank you for those. You ask what will it do to secure improvements. I've got to just remind you that responsibility and accountability for delivery of day-to-day services is still held by the health boards. I don't personally run the health board or go in there and dictate what staff do or what theatre spaces are used and so forth. That's why we have to make sure that we have a system in place that people can have confidence in, that is transparent, where people know what the issues are, and that is consistent across Wales, and that's what we're putting in place here.

Following up on part of the question that you asked at the end there, which was what the problem was with the previous framework, it's exactly that—there wasn't confidence in it. I wrote a paper on this three years ago. It's in the library upstairs if you want to go and read it. It's a very good paper. So, it shouldn't come as a surprise that we're doing this. The health boards, trusts and organisations didn't have confidence in that process, because they didn't know by what criteria they were being escalated or downgraded. There wasn't transparency around that. One health board had a different criteria set to another health board. So, we needed to set in place a consistent process whereby everybody knew what they were being measured against, which is what we're doing here.

Running at the best part of 20 pages with a lot of detail in it, it is a comprehensive framework, and it will be reviewed over the next 12 months. So, you can have confidence that any lessons from implementing it that need to be learned will be learned over the next 12 months. I would, in fact, welcome and invite you to provide your own evidence at the end of the process to see if you have confidence in the process along with others within 12 months' time. So, we will be monitoring it over that 12-month period. It won't be, therefore, used as a political football. I can promise you I won't use it as a political football. I want to depoliticise things. That's why we've put transparency central in this new framework.

I welcome the publication of the new accountability and support framework, in particular its emphasis on early identification and purposeful intervention. As Benjamin Hodge Mckenna said, the current framework isn't working. Preventing and making it easier to tackle challenges before they become crises is an approach that I agree with, and I think that everyone in the Chamber would agree with that too. I'm pleased that it's being used in the area of health and our NHS, but also more broadly, as a general guiding principle. 

I hope that the new framework will strengthen accountability and improve services, but given such regional variation in services and performance—something I myself regularly talk about—how will you ensure that the framework is applied consistently across all health boards in Wales, where there is so much variation at present? Thank you.

Croesawaf gyhoeddiad y fframwaith cyfrifoldeb a chefnogaeth genedlaethol newydd, yn enwedig y pwyslais ar ganfod ymyrraeth gynnar ac ymyrraeth bwrpasol. Fel dywedodd Benjamin Hodge Mckenna, dyw'r fframwaith presennol ddim yn gweithio. Mae atal a'i gwneud hi'n haws i fynd i'r afael â heriau cyn iddynt ddod yn argyfwng yn agwedd rwy'n cytuno â hi, a dwi'n meddwl y bydd pawb yn y Siambr yn cytuno gyda hwnna hefyd. Dwi'n falch ei fod e'n cael ei ddefnyddio ym maes iechyd a'r gwasanaeth iechyd, ond hefyd yn fwy eang, fel egwyddor arweiniol cyffredinol. 

Gobeithiaf y bydd y fframwaith newydd yn cryfhau cyfrifoldeb ac yn gwella gwasanaethau, ond o ystyried y gwahaniaethau mawr yn rhanbarthol mewn gwasanaethau a pherfformiad—rhywbeth dwi fy hun yn siarad yn aml amdano—sut byddwch chi'n sicrhau bod y fframwaith yn cael ei gymhwyso'n gyson ar draws pob bwrdd iechyd yng Nghymru, lle mae cymaint o amrywiaeth? Diolch yn fawr.

contributions.text_english:
Thank you, Gwyn, for those questions. And I'm always reluctant to tackle any questions that specialist clinicians such as Gwyn, and, indeed, Safa, can ask, so I'm very pleased that we're talking about something more technical here. 

But the Member is perfectly right to note that early intervention is a core part of this Government's principles—ensuring that we recognise problems and that we tackle them before they arise. And that's why this is central to the new framework. But how do we ensure that there is consistent provision across Wales? Well, that will happen through the fact that we will gather stakeholders—Healthcare Inspectorate Wales, Audit Wales, Welsh Government, and the health boards themselves—in order to have that consistency when issues arise, and that it'll be undertaken through NHSPI, and that it's all public. 

In terms of consistency, one element that won't be consistent, perhaps, every time is that different regions will have unique problems, and that the health boards will provide input into that process. So, there will be slightly different elements in terms of enabling for those regional differences, but the framework will be consistent across Wales.

Diolch yn fawr iawn, Gwyn, am y cwestiynau yna. A dwi’n gyndyn bob tro o fynd i’r afael ag unrhyw gwestiynau y mae clinigwyr arbenigol fel Gwyn, ac, yn wir, Safa, yn medru ymgymryd â nhw, felly, dwi’n falch ein bod ni’n sôn am rywbeth mwy technegol fan hyn.

Ond mae’r Aelod yn berffaith gywir, Lywydd, i nodi bod ymyrraeth gynnar yn greiddiol i egwyddor y Llywodraeth yma—gwneud yn siŵr ein bod ni’n adnabod problem ac ein bod ni’n mynd i’r afael ag e cyn ei fod o’n digwydd. A dyna pam mae hynna yn ganolog i’r fframwaith newydd yma. Ond sut mae sicrhau bod cysondeb yn y ddarpariaeth ar draws Cymru? Mi fydd hwnna trwy’r ffaith ein bod ni’n ymgynnull rhanddeiliaid—HIW, fel dwi’n dweud, Archwilio Cymru, Llywodraeth Cymru, a’r byrddau iechyd eu hunain—er mwyn cael y cysondeb yna pan fo materion yn codi, a'i fod o’n cael ei weithredu gan NHSPI, a bod hwnna i gyd yn gyhoeddus.

Nawr, o ran y cysondeb, yr un elfen na fydd yn gyson, hwyrach, drwy’r amser yw bod problemau unigol, unigryw yn mynd i fod mewn rhanbarthau gwahanol, a bod y byrddau iechyd yn rhoi mewnbwn yn y broses yma. Felly, bydd yna elfennau ychydig yn wahanol er mwyn galluogi ar gyfer y gwahaniaethau rhanbarthol, ond mi fydd y drefn, y fframwaith a'r system yn gweithio oddi fewn yn gyson ar draws Cymru.

I thank you, Minister, for your statement, and, genuinely, I hope this does work, for all of my constituents in Clwyd, but also for myself and my family. Certainly, with Betsi Cadwaladr health board, you never quite know when you're going there what's going to happen, and we've had some horror stories over the last 12 months, particularly.

But I just wanted to focus on this idea of health boards setting their own criteria and the assessments being made by stakeholders. I'm just a bit concerned about that, because, obviously, there's senior management in place right now, and chief executives in place right now, who are overseeing health boards that really aren't doing a good enough job. And you're sort of asking them to mark their own homework. I'd hope they would be very nervous about this framework coming in and they'd need to pull their socks up. Because this is about leadership and culture. So, that's down to human beings inside organisations just not doing a good enough job, and trying to change that culture has to be carrot and stick. So, I'm slightly concerned about them setting their own criteria, so a little bit more about that, please. 

And then, in terms of making the public aware of what we're doing, it's a pretty dry document, isn't it? And it's trying to make sure that the public understand that all of us want to make sure the NHS is a much better-run organisation. How are we going to get that across to the public about these changes? And, particularly, I was interested that the accountability review may be held in public for health boards. So, tell us a little bit more about that, and about setting your own criteria. Diolch.

Diolch, Louise. Very good points there. You're very, very right, it's a dry document, isn't it, and I think it shows in the numbers present here. It's not, probably, the most exciting thing, but it's one of the foundational pieces of work that we have to get to grips with if we're going to see improvement in the health service in Wales, hence why we've commissioned the work and we're announcing it today. 

It's not that health boards will be setting their own criteria; they'll be working with HIW, Audit Wales and the Welsh Government, who will be key stakeholders in that. But what we want is for health boards to take ownership and be answerable for problems in their health boards, rather than wash their hands of it and deny any responsibility and try and palm it off to somebody else.

So, we want health boards, and trusts as well, to realise, if there is a problem, they identify it—we identify it early, collectively, we put in place the intervention measures required to deal with it at an early stage before it escalates, and then they can move on in confidence that that problem has been dealt with at an earlier stage. That's why they have to be key in identifying those problems. It's not that they say, 'Well, we think that this problem is small and we're not going to deal with it.' It's taking ownership, answerability and accountability—crucial when it comes to ensuring that we have improvement in the health service.

I welcome the fact that you're hopeful that this will work. I think we're all hopeful that it will work. And I'm confident that we've got a new framework in place that will ensure clarity, consistency and transparency, and that it will hold health boards to account far more than the previous framework that we had.

Thank you for that. I am disappointed that you're taking this opportunity to make political points on issues that are beyond what we're addressing today. You know full well that the Government can't intervene in the process that is currently ongoing when it comes to reviewing healthcare provision in Powys or in any other health board. I would hope that everyone present would be entirely aware of the rules saying that a Minister cannot intervene in that process; it's been well known for a very long period of time. So, I'm not going to discuss the process that's ongoing in Powys at the moment.

Powys is at level 4 in relation to the current escalation framework when it comes to budget, strategy and planning. That's a decision that was made by stakeholders, as I've mentioned. And once again, when it comes to looking at the provision of health services in Powys in its entirety, just like any other health board, they will be measured according to the same system as every other health board. But I would encourage people to get in touch if they have concerns about what's happening in terms of the recommendations in Powys. No decision has yet been made—it is a live process. So, if people want to contribute to that process, then do so, contact the health board. More than that, contact Llais—ensure that Llais is aware of any concerns or support that you may have. I've made it clear, in terms of any reorganisation of services in any region in Wales, that we must take into account factors like rurality, local transport, access to services. All of these have to be considerations as any health board draws up its local health services plan in their area.

contributions.text_english: Thank you, Cabinet Minister. I welcome this new national accountability and support framework. In the past, we've seen organisations remain in escalation for years without it being clear that the intervention itself was delivering improvement. I'm particularly concerned about Hywel Dda health board, where finance, strategy and planning, and urgent and emergency care, have risen to level 4. Digital Health and Care Wales, which should be helping to transform services and deliver sustainable solutions, actually moved from level 1 in 2024 to whole-organisation level 4 intervention in April 2026. So whilst, Cabinet Minister, I welcome the emphasis on prevention, transparency and better outcomes, how will you ensure that this new framework creates the space needed for leadership and for investment for the long term so it does make meaningful, sustainable change for patients? Diolch.

contributions.text_english: Thank you very much to Anna Nicholl for that series of hugely important questions when it comes to looking at how we ensure that we create that space to improve leadership. Leadership is at the heart of this new framework. It is one of those things where we are aware, if the culture is right from the top down, then that will lead to better results across the board. The Member is right in saying that Hywel Dda is at level 4, and, indeed, level 3 for planned care, and, indeed, Digital Health and Care Wales is in level 4 too. So, not one of the health boards is in an ideal position. We don't want to see them in this position. The framework that we've drawn up is one that goes as far as possible within the legislative frameworks available to us, namely the National Health Service (Wales) Act 2006, the National Health Service Finance (Wales) Act 2014, the Health and Social Care (Quality and Engagement) (Wales) Act 2020, and the Well-being of Future Generations (Wales) Act 2015. Within all of those, and the other frameworks, this will take us as far as possible in terms of holding the health boards to account, but, more than that, ensure that there is early identification of any problems, that support is provided, and that we take the health boards on an improvement journey so that— exactly as you said—we improve outcomes for the people of Wales. Because the intention is no longer to point the finger and to criticise and to use the escalation framework as a political tool; our intention now is to create a framework that will take health boards on a journey in order to improve outcomes for the people of Wales, from Anglesey to Monmouthshire.

Thank you very much, Dirprwy Lywydd. Today, I'm pleased to inform Members that I've launched a national conversation about the future of Wales through the creation of a new national development framework. The national development framework sits at the heart of the planning system in Wales, providing the strategic direction for regional and local development plans, and the framework for planning and development decisions across Wales. As Wales continues to respond to significant challenges, including climate change, nature recovery, housing need, economic growth and infrastructure delivery, it's essential that our national planning framework is fit for purpose and capable of supporting our nation's ambitions for the future.

Within the first 100 days of this new Government, a public consultation was launched marking the start of the process for revising the framework and beginning a national conversation about the long-term future of Wales. Rather than consulting solely on planning matters, engagement work throughout the process will invite people to consider the long-term future of Wales and the role that places, communities, infrastructure, the environment, the Welsh language and culture should play in shaping our nation's future to 2050.

We are inviting the people of Wales to help shape the direction, priorities and scope of the new national development framework. This reflects our commitment to work with local authorities, regional partners and stakeholders across Wales to develop a framework that meets Wales's needs, empowers local government, and reduces costs, bureaucracy and duplication. It also supports our ambition to move towards a community-centred approach to planning, giving communities a real say on how we secure the homes, the workplaces and infrastructure they need. The framework will play a key, overarching role in how those decisions are made locally, regionally and nationally.

Importantly, the national conversation will also help co-ordination across a range of plans and strategies that are being taken forward during this Government term, as outlined in our programme for government that was published last week. This collaborative and co-ordinated approach to align national priorities will ensure more effective delivery of Government objectives.

The decisions made through the planning system touch every aspect of daily life. They influence where homes are built, how people travel, where businesses invest, how energy is generated and distributed, and how we protect and enhance our natural environment. That is why it's so important that the new national development framework is shaped by a broad range of voices, experiences and evidence. I want this to be an open, inclusive and meaningful national conversation. The national development framework belongs to everybody, considering its importance in providing a framework for new development across Wales. We welcome and encourage representations from everyone, and every group, institution, business and individual has a contribution to make in developing the national spatial plan.

Alongside the opportunity to submit written representations and submit evidence to support the revision work, the current consultation includes a series of public and stakeholder events across Wales. They'll be taking place in Cardiff tomorrow, on 30 September, Aberystwyth on 6 October and Llandudno on 23 October. They provide the opportunity for all, including local authorities, businesses, developers, infrastructure providers, environmental organisations, housing bodies, community groups, young people and members of the public to have their say and give their views.

Evidence will also play a critical role throughout this process. Through this consultation, I’m inviting stakeholders to contribute information, research, analysis and insight on the opportunities and challenges that Wales is likely to face over the coming decades. This evidence will help inform the preparation of the revised framework, its overall vision, the options that will be considered and the policies contained within it.

At its core, planning is about creating better places for people and the environment. Therefore, the revised national development framework must support sustainable economic growth, resilient communities, environmental stewardship and the long-term well-being of current and future generations. I therefore encourage everyone with an interest in the future of Wales to engage with this consultation and contribute to this important national conversation. Responses can be submitted online, by e-mail or by post until 20 November this year, but there will be more opportunities to engage shortly as well. Thank you.

Diolch yn fawr iawn, Ddirprwy Lywydd. Heddiw, mae'n bleser gen i roi gwybod i'r Aelodau fy mod wedi lansio sgwrs genedlaethol am ddyfodol Cymru drwy greu fframwaith datblygu cenedlaethol newydd. Mae'r fframwaith datblygu cenedlaethol wrth wraidd y system gynllunio yng Nghymru, yn darparu'r cyfeiriad strategol ar gyfer cynlluniau datblygu rhanbarthol a lleol, a'r fframwaith ar gyfer penderfyniadau cynllunio a datblygu ledled Cymru. Wrth i Gymru barhau i ymateb i heriau sylweddol, gan gynnwys newid hinsawdd, adferiad natur, yr angen am dai, twf economaidd a chyflenwi seilwaith, mae'n hanfodol bod ein fframwaith cynllunio cenedlaethol ni yn addas i'r diben ac yn gallu cefnogi uchelgais ein cenedl ar gyfer y dyfodol.

O fewn 100 niwrnod cyntaf y Llywodraeth newydd yma, fe lansiwyd ymgynghoriad cyhoeddus i nodi dechrau'r broses ar gyfer diwygio’r fframwaith a dechrau sgwrs genedlaethol am ddyfodol hirdymor Cymru. Yn hytrach nag ymgynghori ar faterion cynllunio yn unig, fe fydd y gwaith ymgysylltu drwy gydol y broses yn gwahodd pobl i ystyried dyfodol hirdymor Cymru a rôl lleoedd, cymunedau, seilwaith, yr amgylchedd, yr iaith Gymraeg a diwylliant wrth lunio dyfodol ein gwlad hyd at 2050.

Rydym ni’n gwahodd pobl Cymru i helpu i lunio cyfeiriad, blaenoriaethau a chwmpas y fframwaith datblygu cenedlaethol newydd. Mae hyn yn adlewyrchu ein hymrwymiad i weithio efo awdurdodau lleol, partneriaid rhanbarthol a rhanddeiliaid ledled Cymru i ddatblygu fframwaith sy'n diwallu anghenion Cymru, yn grymuso llywodraeth leol, ac yn lleihau costau, biwrocratiaeth a dyblygu. Mae hefyd yn cefnogi ein huchelgais i symud tuag at ddull cynllunio sy'n canolbwyntio ar y gymuned, gan roi llais go iawn i gymunedau ar sut rydym ni’n diogelu'r cartrefi, y gweithleoedd a'r seilwaith sydd eu hangen arnynt. Fe fydd y fframwaith yn chwarae rôl gyffredinol allweddol yn y ffordd y mae'r penderfyniadau hynny'n cael eu gwneud yn lleol, yn rhanbarthol ac yn genedlaethol.

Yn bwysig, fe fydd y sgwrs genedlaethol hefyd yn helpu i gydlynu ar draws ystod o gynlluniau a strategaethau sy'n cael eu symud ymlaen yn ystod tymor y Llywodraeth hon, fel yr amlinellir yn ein rhaglen lywodraethu a gyhoeddwyd yr wythnos diwethaf. Bydd y dull cydweithredol a chydgysylltiedig yma o alinio blaenoriaethau cenedlaethol yn sicrhau bod amcanion y Llywodraeth yn cael eu cyflawni'n fwy effeithiol.

Mae'r penderfyniadau a wneir drwy'r system gynllunio yn cyffwrdd â phob agwedd ar fywyd bob dydd. Maen nhw’n dylanwadu ar ble mae cartrefi yn cael eu hadeiladu, sut mae pobl yn teithio, ble mae busnesau yn buddsoddi, sut mae ynni yn cael ei gynhyrchu a'i ddosbarthu, a sut rydym ni’n diogelu ac yn gwella ein hamgylchedd naturiol. Dyna pam mae hi mor bwysig bod y fframwaith datblygu cenedlaethol newydd yn cael ei siapio gan ystod eang o leisiau, profiadau a thystiolaeth. Dwi am i hon fod yn sgwrs genedlaethol agored, gynhwysol ac ystyrlon. Mae'r fframwaith datblygu cenedlaethol yn perthyn i bawb o ystyried ei bwysigrwydd wrth ddarparu fframwaith ar gyfer datblygiadau newydd ledled Cymru gyfan. Rydyn ni’n croesawu ac yn annog sylwadau gan bawb, ac mae gan bob grŵp, sefydliad, busnes ac unigolyn gyfraniad i'w wneud wrth ddatblygu'r cynllun gofodol cenedlaethol.

Ochr yn ochr â'r cyfle i gyflwyno sylwadau ysgrifenedig a chyflwyno tystiolaeth i gefnogi'r gwaith diwygio, mae'r ymgynghoriad presennol yn cynnwys cyfres o ddigwyddiadau i'r cyhoedd a rhanddeiliaid ledled Cymru sy'n cael eu cynnal yng Nghaerdydd yfory, 30 Medi, yn Aberystwyth ar 6 Hydref ac yn Llandudno ar 23 Hydref. Maen nhw’n rhoi cyfle i bawb, gan gynnwys awdurdodau lleol, busnesau, datblygwyr, darparwyr seilwaith, sefydliadau amgylcheddol, cyrff tai, grwpiau cymunedol, pobl ifanc ac aelodau o'r cyhoedd i gael lleisio eu barn.

Bydd tystiolaeth hefyd yn chwarae rôl hanfodol drwy gydol y broses yma. Drwy'r ymgynghoriad yma, dwi’n gwahodd rhanddeiliaid i gyfrannu gwybodaeth, ymchwil, dadansoddiad a mewnwelediad ar y cyfleoedd a'r heriau y mae Cymru yn debygol o’u hwynebu dros y degawdau nesaf. Bydd y dystiolaeth hon yn helpu i lywio'r gwaith o baratoi'r fframwaith newydd, ei weledigaeth gyffredinol, yr opsiynau a fydd yn cael eu hystyried a'r polisïau fydd yn cael eu cynnwys ynddo.

Yn ei hanfod, mae cynllunio yn ymwneud â chreu lleoedd gwell i bobl a'r amgylchedd. Felly, rhaid i'r fframwaith datblygu cenedlaethol newydd gefnogi twf economaidd cynaliadwy, cymunedau gwydn, stiwardiaeth amgylcheddol a lles hirdymor cenedlaethau'r presennol a'r dyfodol. Felly, dwi'n annog pawb sydd â diddordeb yn nyfodol Cymru i fod yn rhan o'r ymgynghoriad yma a chyfrannu at y sgwrs genedlaethol bwysig yma. Mae modd cyflwyno ymatebion ar-lein, drwy e-bost neu drwy'r post, hyd at 20 Tachwedd eleni, ond mi fydd yna fwy o gyfleon i ymgysylltu maes o law hefyd. Diolch.

contributions.text_english:
Thank you to the Minister for her response this afternoon. Minister, Wales is not short of plans, it is short of homes, though, and this statement offers the people of Wales potentially four more years of plans. So, this really is just a plan for a plan.

The Minister has told us that this revision will cut costs, bureaucracy and duplication, and I certainly welcome that, Minister, but I've read your party's manifesto, and it points in a completely opposite direction. Plaid promised Welsh language impact assessments in the planning system. They've promised community ownership stakes in larger energy companies, a new Welsh water regulator and a review of second homes and holiday lets, not to mention a new climate and nature action plan. Some of these, though, Minister, are not mentioned in this statement. But every one of those is another piece of red tape, another stakeholder, more paperwork for local sites to wade through, and another reason for planners to say 'no'.

So, firstly, can the Minister tell this Chamber which of these new layers is she prepared to drop in the name of efficiency, which she wants? Because the numbers demand it. When 'Future Wales' was adopted, the Government said that Wales needed 7,400 homes a year. In 2024-25, we built under 5,000, and last year we built just over 5,000, still well below the levels pre-pandemic. Her own experts now say we need 8,700 a year. We in Reform said plainly during the election that Wales needs at least 10,000 additional homes just to catch up. So, I ask the Minister: will this framework finally contain a delivery figure for all tenures that this Senedd can hold her and the Government to account on? And we need to include all tenures because, as I mentioned before, Minister, 83 per cent of Welsh homes are owner-occupied or are private rented accommodation, yet this Government acts like the private sector is irrelevant. Almost every housing headline this Government produces is about social housing, about speeding up development for social housing or anything that ticks the box for net zero.

This country already has one of the largest housing stocks in Europe for social housing. So, in the framework, will the Minister rule out any two-tier systems for private and social, making sure that any cuts to red tape also apply to private developments, to help the majority who are private renters and mortgage holders, because, Minister, private developers deliver almost half of so-called affordable housing? Of course, the only way to have generally affordable housing is by making sure that market supply actually meets demand. Thank you very much for those comments, and thank you in particular for the ideas that you put forward at the end of your contribution—those ideas on practical steps that could be taken. That's the exact purpose of this consultation: to invite people like you, like all of us in this Chamber, to give serious consideration to how we can improve the planning system so that it can respond more quickly to planning applications when problems arise with the issues that you mentioned in your contribution. So, there are a few ideas there that are worth looking into, and I would encourage some of you who are interested in this area—many of us have been county councillors and are highly aware that the planning system can sometimes hold back housing development. That is exactly why we are carrying out this consultation.

It is a consultation on how the planning process needs to be made more effective and efficient, but it is also a consultation on our long-term vision for Wales. The reason for doing this is that we feel that, during the existence of this Senedd, a clear direction in terms of the future of our nation hasn't been adequately apparent. So, there is an opportunity, with a new Government, to use the process that exists in statute already, namely the reform of the national planning framework, to have that conversation with the people of Wales on the long-term future of our nation.

Plaid Cymru firmly believes in building Wales, in building the nation, and creating a Wales that works for the people of Wales, connecting Wales more effectively in terms of transport, for example. That isn't happening at the moment, as anyone who travels around our country will know. We are not well connected, so transport comes into this consultation.

There is an opportunity to discuss energy policy too. We know that we are facing challenges in moving forward with more renewable energy developments. So, under this framework, there are a number of different plans that will sit underneath it. And I understand the comments that you make about plans and strategies, and so on, and I share some of that frustration. What we want is action, to see things happening. But they have to happen in a co-ordinated way and in a way that has been properly discussed in terms of the long-term direction of travel that we want to see for our nation. I don't think that 'Future Wales', the current plan, provides that clear picture as to what kind of future Wales needs. And certainly, 'Future Wales', the existing plan, hasn't been able to identify some of the major challenges, some of which are developing as we speak, of course, because the plan is old, and there are new challenges coming to face us all the time and we must, therefore, reform in order to take into account all those other issues that are part of our vision for developing our nation. Thank you.

Dyna'n union ydy pwrpas yr ymgynghoriad yma: i wahodd pobl fel chi, fel pawb ohonom ni yn y Siambr yma, i feddwl o ddifrif am sut allwn ni wella'r gyfundrefn gynllunio fel ei bod hi'n gallu ymateb yn gynt i geisiadau cynllunio pan fydd yna broblemau yn codi efo'r materion roeddech chi'n sôn amdanyn nhw. Thank you, Cabinet Minister, for your statement here today. Let me start by saying that it is a good thing that the Government is in listening mode, but having said that, this national conversation can't become an excuse for Ministers not to act and nor can it be allowed to hold up delivery elsewhere. So far, this Government's instinct has too often been to announce reviews and outsource decisions, rather than take the action needed. We've already seen more than 30 talking shops, reviews and expert panels announced, but precious little action, and planning is an area where we really need that speedy reform, not least to build the homes that Wales needs and to power the clean energy revolution. So, Cabinet Minister, can you confirm that the Government will use every lever available through the planning system to support the growth of Wales's renewable energy sector?

Cabinet Minister, you also said today that this national conversation will help co-ordinate a range of plans and strategies in the programme for government. But can you explain exactly what that means? Are other Government policies dependent on the outcome of this conversation, and if so, which ones?

Lastly, Cabinet Minister, you say that you want this to be an open, inclusive and meaningful conversation, but today, we've heard about just three events across the whole of Wales—in Cardiff, Aberystwyth and Llandudno. So, what reassurance can you provide, Minister, that communities in every part of Wales will have a meaningful opportunity to be heard? And will you commit to publishing what people tell the Government and what policy changes actually come out of this conversation?

Thank you very much, and thank you, Vikki, for welcoming the fact that we are consulting on the national development framework. Certainly, consulting on this doesn't mean that we aren't doing other things in the meantime. With 'Planning Policy Wales', for example, there is a way for us to bring reforms into that policy, as I mentioned previously, in order to move ahead with some of our ambitions swiftly. But I do believe that we need a long-term vision for our nation, and that, in a way, is the opportunity that we have now, and an opportunity to listen to what the people of Wales see as the main challenges. This framework will be a spatial framework, it seems—that's the way of explaining it—so that people can see on a map how the developments in different areas would fit together.

In terms of engagement, the process of engaging on this framework is set out in legislation going back to 2015, before I was in this Senedd, even. During that period, the Planning (Wales) Act 2015 was passed, and there's a requirement in that for the Government to create a national development framework. The Act also sets out the kind of process required in order to reform or create a new framework. Before 2015, there wasn't a statutory national framework. Some of you will remember the Wales spatial plan, but that didn't have any statutory basis. I think it was something to be welcomed when this legislation was introduced. The process of creating and revising the framework is a long-winded one, I would agree with that, and I'm sure that perhaps there's a need to revise that.

We are starting the process today and asking for evidence from every direction. Following that, there will be further opportunities. If you look at the current consultation, it asks questions about whether we're asking the right questions and providing everyone with an opportunity to think, 'We're not asking this, we're not going after this issue, perhaps we should be doing that.' Then there's a process of another consultation. It’s going to take two to three years to take action on it. That’s the Act.

Do I agree with all of that? No, probably not. We should be able to do things much quicker, but that's the situation we are in currently. So, as well as the three workshops, there will be many more opportunities for everybody in Wales to take part and to be part of this conversation. You will be hearing more from me on this subject over the next two to three years.

Mi fydd y fframwaith yma yn fframwaith gofodol, mae'n debyg—dyna'r ffordd i egluro'r peth—er mwyn bod rhywun yn gallu gweld ar fap sut byddai'r datblygiadau mewn gwahanol feysydd yn ffitio at ei gilydd.

Wedyn, mae'r Ddeddf hefyd yn gosod allan y math o broses sydd angen digwydd er mwyn diwygio neu greu fframwaith newydd. Cyn 2015, doedd yna ddim fframwaith cenedlaethol statudol. Bydd rhai ohonoch chi'n cofio'r Wales spatial plan, ond doedd yna ddim statud y tu ôl iddo fo. Dwi'n meddwl roedd hi'n rhywbeth i'w groesawu pan ddaeth y ddeddfwriaeth newydd yma i mewn. Mae'r broses o greu a diwygio'r fframwaith yn un hirwyntog, buaswn i'n cytuno efo hynny, a dwi'n siŵr efallai bod angen diwygio hynny.

Cychwyn y broses ydyn ni heddiw a gofyn am dystiolaeth o bob cyfeiriad. Ar ôl hynny, mi fydd yna gyfleoedd pellach. Os edrychwch chi ar yr ymgynghoriad presennol, mae o'n gofyn cwestiynau ynglŷn ag ydyn ni'n gofyn y cwestiynau cywir ac yn rhoi cyfle i bawb i feddwl, 'Dydyn ni ddim yn gofyn am hyn, dydyn ni ddim yn mynd ar ôl y mater yma, efallai y dylem ni fod yn gwneud hynny.' Wedyn, mae yna broses o ail ymgynghoriad. Mae hwn yn mynd i gymryd dwy neu dair  blynedd i ni weithredu arno fo. Dyna ydy'r Ddeddf.

Ydw i'n cytuno efo hynna i gyd? Nac ydw, mae'n debyg. Mi ddylem ni allu gwneud rhywbeth llawer iawn cynt, ond dyna'r sefyllfa rydyn ni ynddi hi ar hyn o bryd. Felly, yn ogystal â'r tri gweithdy, bydd yna lawer iawn mwy o gyfleoedd i bawb yng Nghymru gymryd rhan a bod yn rhan o'r sgwrs yma. Mi fyddwch chi'n clywed mwy gennyf i ar y pwnc yma dros y ddwy neu dair blynedd nesaf yma.

Can I thank the Cabinet Minister for today's statement? A national development framework should be one of the most important documents produced by our Government. It shapes how and where we build homes, where investment goes, how our transport networks develop, how we support businesses, and, ultimately, what kind of Wales we will leave for our next generation. The Cabinet Minister has described this process as a national conversation about the future of Wales to 2050. I also echo what Vikki Howells just said. Whilst engagement is important, people will rightly expect this exercise to result in real change on the ground, rather than simply another consultation process.

Whilst we welcome the decision to review the current framework, the real question is whether this process will lead to meaningful change or simply result in another strategy document, unless the Government is prepared to follow through with meaningful and measurable reforms, because Wales needs action, not bureaucracy. The Government's own first 100 days plan states that it wants

'a new National Development Framework that...empowers local government and reduces costs, bureaucracy and duplication.' 

Those are objectives that I think many Members across the Chamber could indeed support. The challenge, however, will be whether this Government is prepared to deliver the reforms necessary to achieve them. The Minister has highlighted this review has been launched within the Government's first 100 days. Can she therefore explain what concrete reforms she expects this process to deliver beyond consultation and engagement exercises?

For too long, communities, businesses and local authorities have expressed frustration at a planning system that is often complex, slow and difficult to navigate. We are in the midst of a housing crisis. Too many young people are finding home ownership out of reach. Social housing waiting lists remain too high. Local authorities are under pressure to meet housing demand, whilst balancing infrastructure and environmental considerations. At the same time, businesses often face delays and uncertainty when seeking planning consent for developments that could bring jobs and investments into our local communities.

If this revised framework is to be judged a success, it must help address these challenges. It must support the delivery of more homes in the places people actually want and need them. It must help regenerate our town centres, it must support better transport connectivity and infrastructure, and it must create the conditions for economic growth in every part of Wales.

Planning should be about enabling opportunity, not creating obstacles. Housing must remain a central priority, but this review must also address the wider infrastructure that allows communities to thrive. New homes must be accompanied by transport links, utilities, healthcare provision and employment opportunities. Planning policies should help deliver balanced and sustainable communities, rather than simply allocating land.

The Cabinet Minister has also referred to a national conversation. Of course, it is right that the public should have a voice in shaping the future development of Wales. But that conversation must be rooted in the practical concerns raised by people every day. When I speak to residents, they are concerned about whether their children will ever be able to afford a home in their community. They're concerned about congestion and poor transport links. They're concerned about attracting jobs and investments into their towns and cities. They're also concerned about the future sustainability of their local services. Those are the conversations that really and truly matter. It is essential that local communities feel their voices are genuinely influencing decisions, rather than simply being consulted after key decisions are made already here in the Chamber.

The Government has also spoken about empowering local government. Again, it's a welcome aspiration, but this has to be more than warm words. It means trusting councils and local communities to shape their own future, reducing unnecessary duplication between national, regional and local structures, and it means ensuring that planning decisions are taken as close as possible to the people affected by them. I would therefore welcome further detail from the Minister on what specific planning processes she believes are creating unnecessary duplication, and what additional freedoms local authorities can expect under the new framework.

I hope the Cabinet Minister will ensure this review recognises that different parts of Wales have different challenges. The needs of rural communities are often very different to those of cities. Coastal communities face different pressures from those in the Valleys. A successful framework must recognise those differences, rather than attempting to impose a one-size-fits-all solution from Cardiff Bay.

The Minister also said that the revised framework will help align a range of Government plans and strategies. Whilst better co-ordination is indeed welcome, we must avoid creating additional layers of complexity that slow down decision making, investment and development. The ultimate test of this review will be whether it makes the planning system more effective, more responsive and easier to navigate for communities, businesses and local authorities alike. So, Cabinet Minister, we must approach this process constructively. We will support reforms that reduce bureaucracy. We will support measures that help deliver homes, infrastructure and investment. And we will support genuine efforts to strengthen local democracy and improve planning outcomes.

Ultimately, this review must be judged not by the number of consultations undertaken, reports commissioned or strategies produced, but whether it delivers tangible improvements for communities across Wales. The people of Wales need a planning system that helps build homes, create jobs and strengthen community support as well as economic growth. With that in mind—and my final area of questioning will be on this—can the Minister clarify how local authorities will be given greater influence under the revised framework, what specific measures will be introduced to reduce bureaucracy and duplication, and what timetable the Government is working to for moving from consultation to implementation? That is the standard against which we will assess this Government's proposals. Thank you.

With that in mind—and my final area of questioning will be on this—can the Minister clarify how local authorities will be given greater influence under the revised framework, what specific measures will be introduced to reduce bureaucracy and duplication, and what timetable the Government is working to for moving from consultation to implementation? That is the standard against which we will assess this Government's proposals. Thank you.

contributions.text_english:
Thank you very much, and thank you for raising a number of important points there. Whilst this consultation is ongoing, and it is an important consultation, of course, there is also a great deal of action taking place in this Government. As a mother who brought up four children alone, I know full well what it means to juggle different priorities and to keep many plates spinning simultaneously. So, the suggestion that one simply does one thing and therefore can't do anything else just isn't realistic in my own experience. Many Ministers and I have a whole host of different issues that we are working on as we speak today.

This consultation is one issue that I'm focused on, and I think that's crucially important. But I'm also focusing on delivering the target of 20,000 new social homes by the end of this Senedd term. I welcome your commitment to increasing the social housing stock too. The right for everyone to have a home is at the heart of the work that I am doing in this Senedd. But take a step back now. The development plan and the national development framework also look at issues related to housing. It also looks at issues related to economic growth.

My hope is, having listened and had those conversations, that we will have a new plan that will provide a realistic vision for the development of all parts of Wales. As you mentioned, that's crucially important. The plan and framework must enable us to distribute wealth and growth to all parts of Wales, retaining the economic powerhouses of Cardiff and Newport, but also distributing that economic growth to north, mid and south-west Wales. So, we need meaningful regional strategies too, which will be part of the long-term vision.

You mentioned reducing bureaucracy and planning processes. Well, bring your ideas forward. Everyone tells me that we need to accelerate the planning system, that we need to make things easier, and I agree, and I have some ideas as to how we can make progress in that area. I'm very happy to hear practical ideas as to how we deliver that, in practice, on the ground, so that we do remove some of these barriers that can hold developments back, including crucial housing developments.

I'm looking forward to a new development framework for Wales so that it better serves our people, communities and businesses. Simplifying the planning process will be very welcome and will play a crucial role in increasing economic development and improving productivity. Wales is increasingly being recognised as a strategic location for the infrastructure needed to support the digital economy, but it is essential that the benefits of any investment are felt in the communities affected. Energy and resource consumption is a critical requirement for data centres, and the lack of grid capacity means these developments are often little more than power stations generating electricity from fossil fuels, with industrial-scale diesel generators as backup.

In my own constituency of Caerdydd Ffynnon Taf, a 47 MW gas-fired power station is proposed on the Cardiff east park-and-ride site, in an entirely unsuitable urban location close to schools, care homes and the new Maple Fields housing development. Therefore, the holding directive to give time for Planning and Environment Decisions Wales to consider whether to call in this application is welcome, but communities across Wales are seeking reassurance that we will avoid an unsustainable proliferation of data centres. Please can you provide an update on a specific data centre strategy for Wales as part of the national development framework? Diolch.

Thank you very much. I mentioned at the beginning that there's a need for a new national development framework because there are new challenges and opportunities facing Wales, which was different to the situation in 2015 when this process began, and different to the 2020-21 period, when the framework that still exists today was formed. There are new challenges facing us, and one of those is data centres. I can tell you that the Minister for economy and enterprise, whatever Adam Price's name is now, in his role—. My colleague Adam Price has commissioned work that is going to be looking at data centres and the use of artificial intelligence and so forth, because that specific area lies in his portfolio as Minister.

As I mentioned, this is one of the new things that is coming forward, and it's crucially important that we recognise, with the growth in data centres in Wales, that there is a need for a policy framework that is robust, and one that is going to be useful for the future. Probably we need to do that in a way that provides a balance between the economic benefits, but also recognises the real concerns that people have on a community level, and also the concern about the use of energy and water and so forth, and land use. I think that Adam Price has set out last week that we will be bringing a policy forward as soon as possible. Clearly, it's not appropriate for me to comment on the specific scheme that you've mentioned.

contributions.text_english: Can I thank the Minister for bringing this statement forward? But, Members, this revision will include at least seven different reports, 10 different assessments, and is not expected to be completed until the winter of 2029, a matter of months before the next Senedd election and, possibly, a change of Government, who may then choose to start this process all over again. This timeline is symbolic of the planning system in Wales—broken, costly and painfully slow. For example, planning rules require councils to decide on applications within 91 days, but the average wait for a council in my constituency is 223 days. Minister, I often hear from businesses across Wales who point to costly and long waits linked to the planning process as a significant barrier to investment in Wales. Would it not be better to get a grip on the planning crisis at Welsh planning authorities before starting years of work on changing the national framework? We need action now, not a three-year wait. Thank you.

Thank you very much. I do sympathise with your comments. The planning process does take too long. The planning process is complex. The voice of the community isn't heard sufficiently within the process of the development of local development plans, for example. I could go on and on. You as a local councillor will have come across some of those frustrations when we try and get developments through.

I have to say, of course, that planning departments—. Never mind the process itself, the planning departments are under significant pressure in our local authorities. One of the outcomes of years of cuts in public services is cuts to planning services and services of those kinds in order to protect education and social services and so on. So, I have great sympathy with the decline in our planning departments on the ground, and the Royal Town Planning Institute has drawn attention to this in a recent report and is very concerned that we don't have an adequate supply of planners coming through the system, even if we were to change the process, in order to deal with the level of work.

Now, we as a Government are trying to do something to address that issue, and we've supported the work of training new qualified planners across Wales and have created a new bursary scheme jointly with Ceredigion County Council in order to create up to an additional 12 qualified planners in rural areas, where the recruitment challenges are even greater.

So, I agree with some of what you said; I would point out, of course, that there are problems within the system as it's constituted at the moment, but there's now a wonderful opportunity for you to submit your ideas into the consultation—and not just the consultation, write to me, each and every one of you, with your practical ideas as to how we can get developments to move forward more quickly than they do at the moment.

Dydy llais y gymuned ddim yn cael ei chlywed digon o fewn y broses o ddatblygu cynlluniau datblygu lleol, er enghraifft. Mi fedrwn i fynd ymlaen ac ymlaen. Un o ganlyniadau blynyddoedd o dorri ar wasanaethau cyhoeddus ydy torri ar wasanaethau cynllunio ac ar wasanaethau o'r math yna er mwyn, wrth gwrs, gwarchod addysg a gwasanaethau cymdeithasol ac ati. Minister, in contrast to the Reform UK MS, I very much welcome the emphasis on holding a national conversation about the future of planning in Wales. The more people who can engage in that consultation, the better: they are the ones who ultimately will be affected by the planning decisions. Thank you very much for those questions. I think there were two parts to your contribution there. First of all, in terms of engagement and this particular process of creating a new national development framework, I agree entirely with you that we must make a great effort to reach everyone across Wales so that everyone's voice is heard. As I mentioned, this engagement is just the first round, in terms of what will happen before Christmas, and those events have been and are being promoted through third sector groups such as Planning Aid Wales to encourage as many people as possible to participate. Thank you, Deputy Llywydd. Minister, a conversation that closes in November and a framework that arrives in 2029 is not a plan for homes, jobs or high streets now. The current framework already tells north Wales where it sits—national growth in Wrexham and Deeside, while Bangor Conwy Môn is offered only managed coastal growth. If this revision merely re-badges that map, businesses along the A55 will see no change.

Will the Minister confirm three things: first, that the engagement in the north-west will be as serious as in Cardiff; second, that empty and broken high streets will not be treated as lower priority issues; and, thirdly, that this revision will treat Bangor, Caernarfon, Llandudno and Holyhead as more than a supporting act to Wrexham and Deeside and that we won't have to wait until 2029 for a confirmation of that? Conversations do matter, but towns across the north-west cannot wait for the next plan.

I agree entirely with you, as one who represents an area in the very area that you've mentioned in the north-west of Wales, and having represented the area, and having had the privilege of doing so, for over 10 years now. So, you don't need to tell me that communities in the north-west sometimes feel that they are forgotten. This Government won't be forgetting those communities or any community across Wales. That is the vision, ultimately, that I hope can be developed as part of this new framework—that every part of Wales is important and that we need to distribute wealth and economic growth and opportunities across Wales so that we reach every part of the country.

Yes, it's going to take a while, because we are talking about something that is hugely important—the future of our nation. We can't just do it in a week or two; we do have to have those conversations and we need to bring people with us on that journey. But that doesn't mean that we aren't doing other things too. Just tomorrow, I will be meeting the town-centre taskforce, which will be gathering for the first time and that will bring clear recommendations forward by the beginning of next year on some of the challenges facing our town centres, with recommendations on ways of taking action in order to improve our high streets. And there are a number of other, similar issues that are ongoing as we speak.

I've mentioned the taskforce, I've mentioned social housing, there is work happening on retrofitting homes and so on—and that's just in my portfolio. Every Minister can talk to you about at least 10 other things that they are working on today in order to deliver change. But we do have to think of the destination and the future too and not forget, in the midst of those day-to-day important things that we're doing to improve people's lives, that we have to also have a clear vision for building our nation so that it is a nation that is fit for the future, and that brings together the aspirations of everyone here so that we can be far more ambitious in how we go about planning for the future. Thank you.

Dydy'r Llywodraeth yma ddim yn mynd i fod yn anghofio'r un gymuned ar draws Cymru. Dyna'r weledigaeth, yn y pen draw, gobeithio, fydd yn gallu cael ei datblygu fel rhan o'r fframwaith newydd yma—fod pob rhan o Gymru yn bwysig a bod angen dosbarthu cyfoeth, dosbarthu'r twf economaidd a chyfleon economaidd ar draws Cymru i gyrraedd bob rhan.

Ie, mae'n mynd i gymryd sbel, achos rydym ni'n sôn am rywbeth sydd yn bwysig iawn—dyfodol ein gwlad ni. Fedrwn ni ddim jest wneud o mewn wythnos neu ddwy; mae'n rhaid inni fod yn cael y sgyrsiau yna a dod â phobl efo ni yn ystod y sgyrsiau yna. Ond dydy hynna ddim yn golygu nad ydym ni'n gwneud pethau eraill hefyd. Yfory nesaf, dwi yn cyfarfod y tasglu canol trefi, sydd yn ymgynnull am y tro cyntaf a bydd yn dod ag argymhellion clir erbyn dechrau flwyddyn nesaf ynglŷn â rhai o'r heriau sy'n wynebu canol ein trefi ni, efo argymhellion am ffyrdd o weithredu er mwyn gwella ein strydoedd mawr ni. Ac mae yna nifer o faterion fel yna yn digwydd wrth i ni siarad.

Dwi wedi sôn am y tasglu, dwi wedi sôn am dai cymdeithasol, mae yna waith yn digwydd ynglŷn ag uwchraddio tai, retrofit ac yn y blaen—ac mae hwnna jest yn fy mhortffolio fi. Gall bob un Gweinidog sôn wrthoch chi am o leiaf 10 o bethau maen nhw heddiw yn gweithio arnyn nhw, yn gweithio i newid. Ond mae'n rhaid inni feddwl am y pen draw a'r dyfodol hefyd a pheidio ag anghofio, yng nghanol gwneud y pethau dydd i ddydd pwysig iawn yma sydd yn gwella bywydau pobl, fod rhaid inni gael gweledigaeth glir ar gyfer adeiladu ein gwlad ni i fod yn wlad sydd yn ffit ar gyfer y dyfodol, ac sydd yn crynhoi dyheadau pawb yma inni fod yn llawer mwy uchelgeisiol yn sut rydym ni'n mynd ati i gynllunio ac i drefnu'n hunain i'r dyfodol. Diolch.

contributions.text_english: So, I will move on to item 7, a statement by the Deputy Minister for Social Care, Mental Health and Women's Health, improving family-centred neonatal care in Wales, progress towards the Bliss baby charter. I call on the Cabinet Minister for Social Care, Mental Health and Women's Health, Delyth Jewell.
contributions.text_original: Felly, symudaf ymlaen i eitem 7, datganiad gan y Dirprwy Weinidog dros Ofal Cymdeithasol, Iechyd Meddwl ac Iechyd Menywod, gwella gofal newyddenedigol sy'n canolbwyntio ar y teulu yng Nghymru, cynnydd tuag at siarter babanod Bliss. Galwaf ar y Gweinidog Cabinet dros Ofal Cymdeithasol, Iechyd Meddwl ac Iechyd Menywod, Delyth Jewell.

contributions.text_english: Thank you, Dirprwy Lywydd. Today, I am pleased to provide Members with an update on the progress being made across Wales to improve the experience of babies and families receiving neonatal care through the Bliss baby charter. This is a sign of our ongoing commitment to safe, compassionate and equitable services that are centred on families.
contributions.text_original: Diolch, Ddirprwy Lywydd. Heddiw, dwi'n falch o roi diweddariad i’r Aelodau ac i'r Siambr ar y cynnydd ledled Cymru i wella profiadau babanod a theuluoedd sy’n derbyn gofal newyddenedigol, a hynny drwy siarter babanod Bliss. Dyma arwydd o’n hymrwymiad parhaus i wasanaethau diogel, tosturiol a theg, sy’n canolbwyntio ar deuluoedd.

contributions.text_english:
Each year, around 2,800 premature and sick babies in Wales receive neonatal care. For many families, admission to a neonatal unit is one of the most fraught experiences they will ever have to face. Parents may spend weeks or months in hospital dealing with daily uncertainty about their baby's health while they balance travelling to and from the hospital, their job, any other caring responsibilities they have, their family life. 

In those most difficult of circumstances, the care and support that families receive has a lasting impact. Parents need clear information, they need practical and emotional support, and they need to have meaningful opportunities to be involved in their baby's care. Parents should never be treated as visitors but as vital to the care team. Because parents know their baby. They provide comfort, reassurance and continuity, and they have an important role in those decisions about the baby's care. Supporting that relationship is at the heart of the Bliss baby charter and the principles of family integrated care.

I'm so pleased to report that all neonatal units in Wales are now engaged with the charter, either having achieved bronze accreditation or more, or submitted themselves for assessment. The charter is a practical programme that helps services place babies and families at the heart of units. It supports parents to participate in ways that reflect their circumstances and wishes, including hands-on care, involvement in decisions, accessible information and help to remain close to their baby. The charter is not simply about achieving an accreditation award. It gives a structured framework for neonatal teams to recognise good practice, to identify gaps and to agree practical actions for improvement. It encourages services to use families' experiences to shape care and support.

contributions.text_english:
In September 2025, the Welsh Government provided almost £100,000 to Bliss to establish a national neonatal service improvement programme for Wales. Since then, every neonatal unit has either achieved bronze-level accreditation or submitted evidence for assessment under the Bliss baby charter. This marks an important milestone for these services in Wales. However, that is not the end of the story. We have seen further progress: one unit has already achieved silver-level accreditation, and three other units are preparing to submit applications for assessment at this level. Therefore, the commitment of our teams to continuous improvement is abundantly clear. They are keen to ensure that the babies and families receiving their care have a better experience.

Over the past year, Bliss has worked directly with teams in neonatal units across Wales. Units have received support to assess their position against the charter's standards, to carry out reviews and audits, identify local priorities, and develop actions for improvement. Thanks to the programme, services also have the opportunity to share good practice and lessons learned along the way.

Now, not every unit is exactly the same. They vary in size, they vary in the specialist services they provide, and in their facilities, resources, and their staff. They also serve different communities. The charter sets out a national ambition for all units, a shared national ambition, and, at the same time, it allows each individual service to focus on the changes that will make the greatest difference locally.

This would not be possible without the commitment of staff in these units across Wales, and I'd like to pay tribute to the commitment and hard work of those members of staff. Achievement of this programme requires strong leadership and continuous engagement, alongside the daily pressures associated with providing specialist care. Nurses, doctors, allied health professionals, psychologists, support workers and others are working together to place a greater emphasis on including and involving families in the development of services, and delivering meaningful improvements to care.

Ym mis Medi 2025, fe wnaeth Llywodraeth Cymru roi bron i £100,000 i Bliss ar gyfer sefydlu rhaglen gwella gwasanaethau newyddenedigol genedlaethol i Gymru. Ers hynny, mae pob uned newyddenedigol naill ai wedi cyflawni achrediad lefel efydd neu wedi cyflwyno tystiolaeth i’w hasesu o dan siarter babanod Bliss. Mae hon yn garreg filltir bwysig i’r gwasanaethau hyn yng Nghymru. Ond nid dyna ddiwedd yr hanes. Rydyn ni wedi gweld rhagor o gynnydd eto: mae un uned wedi cyflawni achrediad lefel arian yn barod, ac mae tair uned arall yn paratoi i gyflwyno cais am asesiad ar y lefel hon. Felly, mae ymrwymiad ein timau i wella’n barhaus yn gwbl amlwg. Maen nhw’n awyddus i sicrhau bod babanod a theuluoedd sy’n derbyn gofal ganddyn nhw yn cael profiad gwell. 

Dros y flwyddyn ddiwethaf, mae Bliss wedi gweithio’n uniongyrchol gyda thimau mewn unedau dros Gymru gyfan. Mae unedau wedi cael cymorth i asesu eu sefyllfa yn erbyn safonau’r siarter, i gynnal adolygiadau ac archwiliadau, i nodi blaenoriaethau lleol, ac i ddatblygu camau ar gyfer gwella. Diolch i’r rhaglen, mae gan wasanaethau gyfle hefyd i rannu arferion da a’r hyn y maen nhw wedi ei ddysgu ar hyd y daith.

Nawr, dyw pob uned ddim yn union yr un fath. Maen nhw’n amrywio o ran eu maint, maen nhw'n amrywio o ran y ddarpariaeth arbenigol sy’n cael ei chynnig ganddyn nhw, ac o ran eu cyfleusterau a’u hadnoddau, a’u staff. Maen nhw hefyd yn gwasanaethu gwahanol gymunedau. Mae’r siarter yn gosod uchelgais genedlaethol i bob uned ar y cyd, ond mae hi hefyd yn caniatáu i bob gwasanaeth yn unigol ganolbwyntio ar newidiadau a fydd yn gwneud y gwahaniaeth mwyaf yn lleol.

Ni fyddai hyn yn bosibl heb ymroddiad staff yr unedau newyddenedigol ledled Cymru, a hoffwn i dalu teyrnged i ymrwymiad a gwaith caled y staff hynny. Bydd cyflawni’r rhaglen hon yn gofyn am arweinyddiaeth ac ymgysylltu parhaus, ochr yn ochr â’r pwysau dyddiol sy’n gysylltiedig â darparu gofal arbenigol. Mae nyrsys, meddygon, gweithwyr proffesiynol perthynol i iechyd, seicolegwyr, gweithwyr cymorth ac eraill yn gweithio gyda’i gilydd i roi mwy o bwyslais ar gynnwys teuluoedd wrth ddatblygu’r ddarpariaeth, a gwneud gwelliannau ystyrlon i ofal.

contributions.text_english: And we know, of course, that some parents will face additional barriers to being close to or involved in their baby’s care. These could include distance from their home, financial pressures, work, other caring responsibilities, language and communication needs, disability or difficulties in accessing accommodation and practical support. Equity is therefore central to the national programme. Bliss is developing bilingual resources, improving access to information and support for families in Wales, with particular attention to minority ethnic communities and areas of socioeconomic disadvantage. This will help services consider not only whether support is available, but whether every family can understand, can access and can benefit from that support.

contributions.text_english:
The Bliss baby charter supports the quality statement for maternity and neonatal services. This sets out our national vision of providing safe, equitable and person-centred care. The quality statement recommends that health boards should follow the standards of the Bliss baby charter. It also recognises that listening to families' experiences, and involving them, is fundamental to ensuring quality and safety.

The improvements arising from this programme form part, of course, of our wider response to the recommendations set out in 'The path to safer beginnings in Wales' report. That work reinforces the importance of ensuring consistent national leadership arrangements and effective governance. It also confirms how important it is that we genuinely listen to families, while maintaining a strong focus on safety, quality and equity.
contributions.text_original:
Mae siarter babanod Bliss yn cefnogi’r datganiad ansawdd ar gyfer gwasanaethau mamolaeth a newyddenedigol. Hwn sydd yn amlinellu ein gweledigaeth genedlaethol, sef darparu gofal diogel a theg sy’n canolbwyntio ar yr unigolyn. Argymhelliad y datganiad ansawdd yw y dylai byrddau iechyd ddilyn safonau’r siarter. Mae hefyd yn cydnabod bod gwrando ar brofiadau teuluoedd, a’u cynnwys, yn gwbl sylfaenol i sicrhau ansawdd a diogelwch. 

Mae’r gwelliannau sy’n deillio o’r rhaglen hon yn rhan o’n hymateb ehangach, wrth gwrs, i argymhellion adroddiad 'Y llwybr tuag at ddechrau mwy diogel yng Nghymru'. Mae’r gwaith hwnnw yn cadarnhau pwysigrwydd sicrhau trefniadau arweinyddiaeth genedlaethol gyson a llywodraethiant effeithiol. Mae hefyd yn cadarnhau pa mor bwysig yw hi ein bod ni wir yn gwrando ar deuluoedd, gan barhau i ganolbwyntio ar ddiogelwch, ansawdd a thegwch.

contributions.text_english:
Now, while today is an opportunity to recognise progress, the work is not complete. Bronze accreditation is an important foundation, but accreditation must not become an end point. Lasting improvement will depend on units continuing to listen to families, to review their practices, to measure the impact of any changes, and to build on what they have achieved. We have therefore secured continued funding throughout this financial year to further embed the national programme, to support units as they progress through the charter, and to strengthen the sustainability of improvements across health boards. 

During the next phase, Bliss will continue to provide tailored support to neonatal teams and strengthen access to bilingual information for families. Lessons from the programme will build an understanding of where individual units may require further assistance to meet the needs of their local population, and where common barriers may require national action. We will continue to expect clear evidence of progress. Now, as I've said, success cannot be judged solely by whether accreditation is awarded. It must be seen and felt in the experiences of babies and families—whether parents feel welcomed, informed and respected on the ward, whether they can participate in their baby’s care, and whether services listen and respond when families point out that things need to change.

I am really grateful to Bliss for their partnership and their expertise, and to neonatal teams across Wales for their ongoing commitment. Most importantly, though, I thank the parents and families who've shared their experiences and helped to shape this programme for the sake of other families in the future. Their honesty and insight have been invaluable, so too has been their bravery. I am indebted to them and I thank them.

Dirprwy Lywydd, every baby that is born prematurely or is unwell when they’re born deserves the best possible care, and every family deserves to be treated with dignity and compassion. The progress being seen through the Bliss baby charter shows what can be achieved when families, clinicians, health boards, the third sector and Government work together with a shared purpose. Now, we remain committed to supporting neonatal services across Wales to continue this journey to deliver the highest standards of care. Our ambition is clear that neonatal services in Wales should be clinically safe and effective, compassionate and equitable, and genuinely designed around the needs of babies and their families. Diolch.
